speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Due to the decision of the federal Treasury Board to cut back on casual employees at Canadian airports and additional operational cuts ordered recently in Atlantic Canada, forcing airports to restrict runway use during snow and adverse weather conditions this fall and causing vocal concern by some airport managers that the safety of the travelling public may be affected; due to the fact that for the past month, in eliminating a function of air radio operators because of a contract dispute, Transport Canada has ordered runway and approach lighting at some airports in Atlantic Canada to remain at the same intensity regardless of weather conditions, causing pilots to complain of blinding lights during clear weather conditions; and due to the fact that certain of these airports generate revenue through air radio unaccounted for in actual landings, as witnessed by the $3.6 million presently owed the federal government for air radio services supplied in Atlantic Canada to three U.S. airlines, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin):
That the government cancel its ordered maintenance cutback and terirf employee cuts at airports in Atlantic Canada and give air radio operators more recognition in order to protect the safety of the travelling public.

I refer him to a taped conversation which was accepted in the House, and which was accepted when it was referred to in the House, and in particular to a question dated August 23, directed in the latter part of the summer to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the minister
October 19, 1979

who, according to the Prime Minister, was in touch with the United States government all throughout the summer urging the acceptance of the Foothills all-land route. I quote;
Q. Is Canada going to have to re-endorse the Foothills proposal in light of Schlesinger's memo?
Not "any change in Foothills' application" but "Schlesing-er's memo".
A: (Hnatyshyn). Well, I think the position we are taking as a new government is that we are going to review the alternatives and I simply think it is premature to indicate a position on the matter now.
Q. What's the status of the former government's commitment? They said they preferred the Foothills route. Does that stand?
A. Well, 1 think that a new government is going to look at the alternatives and I don't want to suggest that in any way the review itself means that we are either going to change or not change, but I just think the process obviously has to be . . . that we have a chance to look and have a fresh view of all the alternatives and accordingly, when that process is over, our position will be made clear to the United States, to the President of the United States.
This is the minister who, all during the summer, according to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. de Cotret), has been pushing the Foothills route throughout the summer, as stated in Hansard by the Prime Minister. To continue with the taped report:
Q. We have had some technical problems. Could I repeat the question about whether you feel you are under any pressure from the American government to act on this matter?
A. Well, what I have said is that it is my understanding that the Americans, the administration and the new occupants of those positions of energy and the Department of the Interior, are in fact themselves going to look at the whole question and that there is certainly no indication to me, at least based on the information I had at my disposal at the time, of any rejection or acceptance of one alternative or the other.
He was clearly talking about alternatives in the sense of other proposals opposed to Foothills. The answer continued:
So that is still very much open. What I am saying is that I take it that Mr. Schlesinger, in his statement, is expressing his point of view but my understanding is that it is not one that has been accepted as a position of the administration in the United States.
So we find the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources at the end of the summer saying he is taking a fresh look at the whole proposal.
The Prime Minister informed this House that throughout the course of the summer this minister, along with some of his colleagues, had been urging the acceptance of Foothills' proposal.
I would like to quote another minister who was named as urging the acceptance of Foothills' proposal during the course of the summer, as stated by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I refer to the reported remarks of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser) in a story in The Vancouver Sun of October 18, which reads in part as follows:
The Vancouver South MP said in an interview that while the government favours an all-land plan put forward by Foothills Oil Pipe Lines Ltd.-and has gone so far as to say so in a recent aide memoire-
This refers to the aide memoire the Prime Minister said was sent at the end of September.
Privilege-Mr. A l bn and
-"there are more than just environmental considerations'' to take into account.
"Trans Mountain (Pipe Line Co.) at least has the favourable characteristic of getting the tankers out of congested waters''-
The Prime Minister has indicated that this minister throughout the course of the summer had no doubts and was pushing the Foothills' all-land route. This article was made public. It was read, presumably, by the Americans, and it cast doubts. It extolled the virtues of Trans Mountain and a tanker route. Compounding this impression-it is more than an impression; there was a statement by the Prime Minister-was a statement read to this House and which was made by the department of the interior, the lead department, saying that at least halfway through the summer no word had been heard from the Canadian government. The Prime Minister said there were meetings of just officials, let alone officials for ministers during this period.
My question of privilege is this: The Prime Minister of this country today clearly states to this House and to the Canadian people that his ministers-and the government is the Prime Minister and his ministers-have been urging the United States government throughout the summer to accept the Foothills' route. At the end of August the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, one of the lead ministers of this government, said he was looking at all the fresh new proposals and making no commitment with respect to Foothills. This was compounded by the Minister of the Environment who said in Vancouver a week ago that Trans Mountain had its virtues.
It seems to me that this is shoddy, to say the least. I would like some clarification from the Prime Minister because I think this is misleading the House of Commons and the Canadian people.

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege with respect to the wearing of ties in the House of Commons. I put this question of privilege as a serious one. This morning it was my intention to change into a shirt and tie and come here dressed according to

October 19, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Allmand
the traditional rules, but at the last minute I received several important telephone calls.

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like you to hear me out. 1 received important telephone calls, with the result that when the bells rang for the calling of the House I did not have time to change. In the circumstances I thought it was more important to come here without a tie and participate in the proceedings of the House than come late or not at all.
1 really want to question the propriety of this rule-

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext:
If hon. members opposite would be quiet and listen to my argument, I would like Your Honour to reconsider this rule. Parliament is a very old institution, and proper dress in the House of Commons has varied considerably over the 700 or more years Parliament has existed as an institution. For most of those centuries ties in the House of Commons were not the rule. It seems to me that the important thing under the rule of proper decorum in the House of Commons is proper dress and neatness and not necessarily the wearing of ties.
I have visited other Parliaments in the world, and I think that if one inquired of the Parliaments of many countries in the Inter-Parliamentary Union one would find that the wearing of ties is not the rule.
Second, I would like to remind this House that this is a House of Commons. I was just reading the rights and privileges of members of Parliament. This is a house of commoners, and it is my opinion that to the majority of people in Canada common dress is not the wearing of ties, if we consider the total range of population.
The tie I am wearing was lent to me by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar), who is an Inuit. There are Indians and Inuit in this Parliament, and it is not proper to demand the wearing of ties of people whose traditional dress does not include the wearing of ties.
Earlier this week we celebrated "Persons" day which recognized equality between men and women in Parliament. It was a very important anniversary. In this respect I think men in this House should have the same freedom of dress as women.

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext:
1 point out that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) is not wearing a tie today. The hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is not wearing a tie. The hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) is not wearing a tie.
Consequently, I would like Your Honour to reconsider this rule. I think it is anachronistic in 1979 or 1980. I think my constituents want me to be here whether I am wearing a tie or not, and I argue that my privilege to speak as an elected member of Parliament for a constituency was interfered with

merely because I did not have a tie on today, when I wanted to ask a very important question on an important issue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-DRESS OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
speechtext:
Order, please. I do not want to entertain this matter in this way. The hon. member knows that this has been an accepted standard and that standards of dress are very difficult to enforce, define and categorize. For many years all commoners have accepted a standard of dress for men in this House.
I grant that some of the hon. member's representations may be very reasonable. Nevertheless, it has been the accepted standard here by all members of this House of Commons that the standard of dress for men includes ties. I simply say that if the hon. member or any other hon. member wants to try to change that, the right thing to do, surely, would be to do it through their caucuses or perhaps through representations to a committee which might make a recommendation so that the House can change this rule. It is not for me to decide, thank heaven, what the standard of dress should be. The House has made that decision through a long accepted practice, and all I am doing is enforcing it. If the hon. member wants to change it, he should persuade his colleagues, and I will be happy to enforce whatever change there might be. However, until that time comes I am bound to follow the practices of the House as they have been well known to me since I have been here.

MR. BREAU-ALLEGED INSULTING REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege because the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) today, in my view, failed to comply with Standing Order 35 concerning the use of disrespectful and offensive language against members of this House. I therefore rise on a question of privilege to give the Prime Minister the opportunity to clarify the matter because I do not think that any member wants to offend others.
On two occasions today, the Prime Minister made reference to members on this side of the House in a way that could be construed as offensive. First, in reply to a question put by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) regarding House procedures and the legislative program, the Prime Minister stated that some members on this side of the House, some members-he did not specify from which party- had decided to obstruct the budget bills and the business of the House. Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the Prime Minister through you that the budget bills are not yet on the order paper, that no member has seen any, that no one knows if they will be printed in exactly the same format and with the same content as in the last Parliament. Therefore, how can one conclude that members on this side of the House have already decided on the stance they will take during a budget debate or a debate on a budget bill?
October 19, 1979

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is imputing motives, and he did say "some members" without referring to any party. 1 would ask the Prime Minister to clarify his statements and remind him that those summer caucus meetings are over. He is now in the House of Commons in the Canadian Parliament and we expect on this side of the House to scrutinize all the bills he will introduce, whether they be budget bills, bills from the last Parliament or any other bill, first because it is our duty as members to scrutinize the content and presentation of the bills.
The second example I want to deal with in my remarks relates to the arrogant attitude shown today in the House by the Prime Minister, and I would like him to clarify this, Mr. Speaker. At one point, he said in an answer and while looking at me that I had a newly found interest in morality. It may well be that he did not quite understand what I had said, and I would like to give him the opportunity to clarify this, because I do not think he would want to question my political morality, present or past.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure on behalf of my party to inform the House that we are very happy this strike is over. Unfortunately, we cannot congratulate the minister on having settled it himself. I think that attrition and time were the main factors. There is a well-known saying that time is the healer of all ills. It seems indeed that that is what happened in this case, and one cannot say that the Progressive Conservatives are responsible for settling the dispute in the port of Montreal.
That strike which actually lasted several months occasioned heavy expenses and serious inconvenience to farm producers in that area of Quebec. That is what the minister failed to mention this morning. That is what his government wanted to do for them, to compensate them for the extra expenses and inconvenience they suffered because of that strike that lasted too long. It is obvious that the strike pushed up the cost of grain supplies to flour mills, for example and it is obvious the price of feed grains for farm producers increased by several dollars a ton. When my colleague, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Olivier), asked the minister last week what he intended to do about that conflict, he did remind him that this government had intervened immediately right at the start of a similar dispute in western Canada on the Pacific coast. And the hon. member for Longueuil was rightly concerned about the inaction of the Progressive Conservative government about this dispute in the port of Montreal.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) will come to the House later on to tell us what he intends to do to compensate those who were seriously affected by this dispute. In answer to a question by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Ostiguy), the minister said he hoped to be in a position to give fuller information as early as next week, meaning this week, about the breeders who were affected by the strike in the port of Montreal these past months. subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks in the throne speech debate I should like to extend my best wishes to His Excellency the Governor General who presided for the first time at the official

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Yanakis
opening of the Thirty-first parliament. 1 first met Mr. Schrey-er in 1965 when he was member for a Manitoba riding and at that time we were sitting opposite each other in this House. He then served as premier of his province, and in that capacity had a brilliant political career in the service of his fellow citizens, and I wish to offer him, Mr. Speaker, my best wishes in his new office as Governor General of Canada.
I also wish to congratulate the sponsors of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) on the excellent way in which they performed their duty. They gave a fine picture of their ridings and showed that they have much to contribute to Parliament. The new Parliament is made up of newly elected members in all parties, which should give a new impetus to Canadian federalism and prove that the system is still very strong, judging by the calibre of the men and women willing to serve their country. I therefore wish all these newcomers much success in their new responsibilities.
It goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that I am delighted about your appointment to the Chair of this House. The fact you were appointed from an opposition party is unique in the history of our Parliament, and this is all to your credit, because it shows how impartial you have always been. I extend my best wishes to you on this occasion.
Mr. Speaker, in the last election, I was confirmed for a fifth mandate as the representative of my constituency with a record majority in the constituency of Berthier-Maskinonge. This is an honour which, of course, is shared by my family, and it is a token of confidence of my electors towards their member who has been sitting here for 14 years. I want to thank them sincerely and to assure them of my complete dedication in their service and in the service of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, as several hon. members, I was very pleased to hear the Speech from the Throne which was read in the Senate by His Excellency the Governor General. It is the fifth Speech from the Throne I have had the advantage to hear, and I must admit I was very disappointed by this one. Like Canadians, I thought that the new government would give a new impetus to our economy, propose new policies in the area of agriculture, take a new approach to our energy problems, reassure Middle East countries about its long-term foreign policies following the well-known and dramatic blunder made by the Prime Minister when he mentioned the possibility of Canada moving its embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. On the contrary, the Speech from the Throne is entirely lacking in specific references to the orientation of the Clark government foreign policy and the future of our country.
With regard to the Quebec referendum, not a single word, although we all know that since 1867, when the British North America Act was adopted, our country has never been faced with such constitutional problems. Never has the unity of this

country been so threatened. The government did not deem it necessary to even make reference to it, probably believing they would make another mistake they might have to regret, knowing full well that their position on this issue and their policies vis-a-vis the provinces are not very clear. The right hon. Prime Minister prefers not to get his feet wet and capitalize on the joint efforts of the federal and provincial Liberals from Quebec to bring the referendum battle to a successful conclusion, only to claim credit for a moral victory later although not having been involved in the debate.
Indeed, that is the position of the other Tory provinces which are fed up with Quebec's claims within confederation. To show Quebec a spirit of co-operation and a new openness to good understanding, the right hon. Prime Minister has agreed after being in power for five months to give Quebec and the provinces control over the Loto Canada lottery-can you imagine-in return for a tiny monetary compensation which is tantamount to giving the province of Quebec a candy to stop recriminations. This had Mr. Parizeau, the Quebec Minister of Finance, saying that things were finally starting to open up in Ottawa. That is absolutely ridiculous, Mr. Speaker.
During the election campaign, I told my constituents in Berthier-Maskinonge about the danger of electing a Progressive Conservative government, especially one dominated by Western Tory premiers in a particularly difficult period in terms of energy supply. Indeed, as we know, they have the oil.
Five months have elapsed since the Progressive Conservatives took over and we now find ourselves in the midst of an energy crisis. We were told recently by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) that there is not enough oil to supply homes in Eastern Canada next winter. That is all done undoubtedly to make us swallow more easily a substantial increase in the short term, which was not long in coming, Mr. Speaker, given the fact that the minister announced Tuesday night that an increase of 34 cents to 40 cents a gallon of fuel and heating oil was expected for 1980.
Everything is clear now. We wanted to know the position of the Clark government on energy matters. Now we know it, and it is just the beginning. In years to come, we shall be faced with other major increases which will place Canadians, especially those of eastern Canada, in an intolerable situation as regards heating their homes and filling up their gas tanks.
As for us Liberals, our position has always been clear and it still is. We subsidized the consumer, we allowed a price increase which was just enough to stimulate production. This did not please the premiers of oil-producing provinces very much, but we had to consider the needs of all Canadians. It is unwise for the cause of national unity to tell energy-producing provinces that domestic oil prices must reach world levels and that any surplus belongs to them so that they can put into so-called heritage funds billions of dollars at a time when the

eastern provinces fight unemployment and stagnation. These rich provinces have a short memory. They seem to forget their leaner years when all Canada came to their assistance through oil exploration subsidies as well as in the agricultural and transportation fields. What seems even more ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that this new government would like to do a hatchet job on the national corporation of Petro-Canada which was set up by the Trudeau government and received royal assent in July 1975.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are very concerned about the fate of Petro-Canada, as is confirmed by a recent survey among Canadians which shows that they are in favour of leaving untouched this national corporation and several other Canadian public and business companies and corporations. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that any country seriously concerned about securing energy supplies for its citizens will create a national petroleum corporation. In Canada, eight multinational companies share among themselves 91 per cent of our gas and oil. Petro-Canada is a well-administered and efficient corporation with assets of more than $5 billion. It is a profitable corporation which is not afraid of taking risks.
Up to now, those operations have been successful in the Arctic, in Nova Scotia, off Newfoundland and in the west. With Petro-Canada as negotiating agent with Mexico, Venezuela and other oil exporting countries, Canadians have no reason to be afraid of any shortage such as happened last winter when some parts of the country experienced oil shortages because the big multinational Exxon, of which Imperial Oil is a subsidiary, had diverted oil supplies from Canada to the United States.
Now in office, as in many other fields this government is confronted with election commitments, and as it tries to save face, it hesitates to decide what to do about that company. Canadians are not taken in. They will not appreciate the government position in this regard. After five months in power, Canadians are still waiting for those magic formulas the Prime Minister promised during the election campaign to stimulate the economy. As the Prime Minister said solemnly, as we enter the 1980s the ministers were given a mandate to change the direction of Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are off to a shaky start.
Last week the governor of the Bank of Canada announced the third interest rate increase under the new Conservative government, under a Prime Minister who barely nine months ago was going on record as Leader of the Opposition saying that interest rate increases were out of reason. He now agrees with the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey, that U.S. rate increases should be followed, however severe the hardships for the Canadian taxpayer.
Mr. Speaker, in five months since they were elected, interest rates went up three times to a Canadian record. Mr. Clark is learning that he views matters quite differently now that he has to take the decisions instead of criticizing. The government
The Address-Mr. Yanakis
pretend to be looking for long-term solutions but they only do patchwork, as in their interest rate and property tax credit program. It will be interesting to see how the Prime Minister will go about implementing his rather vague program of economic growth. Mr. Speaker, it is stated in the throne speech that the government will have to approve a mortgage interest and property tax credit program.
In his introduction the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) indicated the government wanted to free the people in order to strengthen liberty. What he forgot is that the only way to free the people is to bring down social and economic barriers, but there is no sign of that in the throne speech.
There are in this country millions of people who are forgotten, unthought off, neglected and even despised. There is nothing for them in the throne speech. What this government is doing is raising barriers and emphasizing divisions. Quite the contrary, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) indicates the election promise of mortgage rate tax credit will benefit
300,000	Canadians who will have a stake in the country. He suggests this will stimulate employment and have economic spin-offs. He forgets to say what is in store for the remaining 40 per cent of the people in rental housing in Canada and the 60 per cent in Quebec. This program brings them no direct benefit. The minister seems to be saying that since he promised them nothing he does not have to think about them. The only people who count for this government are those to whom it made promises; others do not count.
Mr. Speaker, I remember that when Senator Edward Kennedy came to visit Ottawa, two or three years ago, to consult our Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on our hospital and health insurance program, which he wanted to introduce in the United States, in answer to a question concerning the tax credit on mortgages, he suggested that we do not embark on this program which is already implemented in the United States, and does far more harm than good there for most people.
In fact, this program helps mostly people with upper middle or high incomes. I am not surprised, Mr. Speaker, that this Progressive Conservative government persists in going through with this policy notwithstanding much advice to the contrary, because this Progressive Conservative government wants to preserve its tradition of legislating in favour of the rich at the expense of the working people.
Mr. Speaker, I was saying at the beginning of my remarks that there was not a single word about agriculture in the throne speech, and God knows that when the Progressive Conservatives were in opposition they knew all the answers to our agricultural problems. After five months in power, nothing, not even the hope of a new policy in the throne speech. Canada is renowned as the granary of the world with its cereal crops, particularly in the west. Furthermore, it is known as one

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Yanakis
of the great cattle producers in the world, and in the eastern part of the country the dairy farmers produce almost all the natural milk, industrial milk, butter and cheese, not to mention poultry farmers as well as beef and pork producers.
The government did not think once about helping them face the ever-rising cost of feed products and administration. Concerning the crucial problems of the agricultural economy about which the Progressive Conservatives were so concerned when they were in opposition, not one word in the throne speech, as if all our farmers suddenly became prosperous and the government had to consider other priorities.
Mr. La Salle, who is not in the House today, has not treated me as courteously as I did last week when I listened to his speech. Last Tuesday he attempted to bring the agricultural issue into perspective by taking credit for the dairy policy proposed by the Liberal government when he announced the reimbursement of export taxes amounting to $26 million and the readjustment of milk quotas on the basis of consumption.
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the silence of his government in the Speech from the Throne, which, I am sure, will provoke smiles among the farmers of his Joliette riding and the Delanaudiere area where 1 come from, particularly also among the members of APU, Mr. La Salle discussed the dairy policy support program while he attempted to take credit for it. The objectives of that policy are, first, to establish quotas for industrial milk on the basis of Canadian demand in order not to flood the consumer market and to protect producers; second, to index the subsidy paid to industrial milk producers on the basis of inflation costs and production cost increases; and third, to hand back to producers the levy of 20 cents a hundredweight on deliveries to absorb the export cost of production within the quotas set for producers.
This is where those $26 million are coming from. It is not a subsidy, it is just a deposit which producers have left in the hands of the Canadian Dairy Commission and which will be repaid to them very soon. There was nothing new in all this as the subsidies established by the Liberals under the dairy policy is a statutory program that was always criticized by the Progressive Conservatives. But they have yet to propose an alternative. Instead the minister should have announced at the opening of this Parliament the new agricultural policies proposed by the Progressive Conservatives to assure a balanced operational income to our farmers in a period when inflation is so high.

In his speech the hon. Minister of Supply and Services said that when the Liberals were in power the number of unemployed reached 1,500,000. I just wonder where he got those figures. To him the value of figures is irrelevant. What he is interested in, Mr. Speaker, is simply to mystify people as he is used to. Right now, thanks to the last budget presented by Mr. Chretien, the former minister of finance in the former Trudeau cabinet, the number of unemployed has been lowered to nearly 700,000 and the national rate is down to 7 per cent for a workforce of 10,300,000 Canadians. That is the truth, Mr. Speaker, and in his new position the minister should know that he cannot juggle figures as he sees fit because people are not fooled so easily. I challenge the Progressive Conservative government to improve in the coming months the situation, especially the economic situation in which it has put us since it came to power.
Mr. Speaker, I could speak at length on the legislative program of this government but I notice that my time is running out. Canadians keep their eyes wide open on the Clark government whose actions have already started to create much scepticism among the public, among businessmen and our international partners. The hesitations of the government, the Prime Minister's untimely statements on the issue of the move of our embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, his energy policy
October 19, 1979

which is bound to increase the cost of living and will fuel current inflation, his indifference towards the Quebec referendum, his monetary policy are already very expensive for Canadians although this government has only been in power for five months. We are still waiting for the prophetic Prime Minister who was to work miracles and cure the ills of our economy. In the 1980s he will have to act otherwise we in the opposition will have to turf out the government. Mr. Speaker, just before lunch 1 indicated that 1 intended to join in this throne speech debate largely to outline certain of the realities that faced the nation with respect to the former government's spending plans and the current government's spending plans.
Before I get into the main body of those remarks, I feel I should like to join the many others who have congratulated the House on the selection of the new Speaker to carry on as he did in the earlier Parliament.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) for their excellent addresses in moving and seconding the motion that is now before us.
Of course, 1 should also like to indicate my encouragement to you as Deputy Speaker for accepting your new role, as well as the appointment of the Speaker to which 1 have referred.
I feel that in considering the throne speech, which I would
mention was extended or certainly elaborated upon by the
The Address-Mr. Stevens
Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) in this debate, it is particularly important that we as members of Parliament consider the reality of Canada's spending position at the present time. As you know, Mr. Speaker, on October 11 I tabled various documents in this House including the main estimates for the fiscal year 1979-80. We also tabled supplementary estimates A to those main estimates. Before the middle of November we intend to table supplementary estimates B, and it is anticipated that before the end of this fiscal year there will be a further tabling of supplementary estimates C.
The reason I mention that is that I feel it is important, as we consider the spending plans of this government, which are to some degree an extension of the plans of the former government, that we be candid with the Canadian public as to what is the reality of Canada's fiscal position at the present time. I say that because you will recall that when I was tabling, in the rather routine way that it is done, the main estimates for the current fiscal year, the House leader for the opposition party seemed to chide or somehow or other try to get me to say whether I "approve", to use his word, or recommend the main estimates to this House. 1 was very curious why the House leader for the opposition would have chosen that day to appear to be, if not naive, rather childish, knowing as he does that it is certainly not traditional for the person who simply tables the main estimates to make some statement that he recommends them or approves them.
I therefore felt it was perhaps important that I reflect on what the hon. member really had in mind when he made that request. Naturally, knowing that he is a great scholar of the English language, I thought 1 had better go to the Oxford dictionary to see what in fact is meant by the word "recommend". I think it is interesting to get that on the record. Oxford says that to recommend is to give in charge to God a person, his care, etc.; to speak or write of in favour or trial; say something is fit. When we turn to the word "approve", we find it means to confirm, sanction, commend, pronounce or consider good.
When you think of the significance of those two words as defined in the Oxford dictionary, I am a little pressed to understand why the House leader used the word "recommend". If in fact what he was seeking was an approval, what he was in effect asking me to do was to refer the main estimates and confirm them, sanction them, commend them, pronounce them or consider them good.
I had been very careful when I tabled those main estimates to make it clear that they were exactly as tabled in February this year by the previous government. We had taken that very, very conscious step because we believed, as the ongoing process of this House would evolve, that it was necessary, certainly from a procedural standpoint, to get those estimates reintroduced for consideration by the House. Frankly, if the House leader feels any better on that basis as part of the ongoing process of this House, I recommend them to the House and that they get on with them.

October 19, 1979

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

The thing I think we have to make very clear is that those main estimates, as it has now evolved, are only part of the ongoing considerations that this House must bear in mind concerning the over-all spending plans certainly of the former government and currently of this present government. There are four things I would suggest that hon. members bear in mind as they work their way through the main estimates, the supplementary estimates A and supplementary estimates B. Those four things are as follows.
[DOT] (M10)
Hon. members will note that I received first reading today with respect to a bill to alter the accounts of Canada. I am going to touch on that a little more fully later. It is a sad story. We have found, largely through the work of the Comptroller General of Canada, that the previous government was recording various assets as being realizable assets on the part of the Government of Canada when in fact there was no net worth there.
We feel the time has come to make some of these revelations. We are not talking about nickels and dimes. We are no longer talking about "What's a million?" We are talking about "What's a billion?" The amount of the write-off that this House is going to be asked to consider with respect to the fiscal year 1978-79 is now over $4 billion. When we look at these main estimates which were first tabled in February of this year, there was absolutely no indication by the government of the day that there was serious doubt with respect to some of the assets they were still recording as being fair assets on the part of the Government of Canada and which, if they had written them off in the 1979 fiscal year, would have indicated their deficit was up by over $4 billion. That was never revealed.
Second, it is important to bear in mind that in considering the main estimates one must consider supplementary estimates A, which have already been tabled in this House. I would suggest, and hon. members will have ample time to do this, that they also consider supplementary estimates B, which will be introduced certainly early enough to allow hon. members to look at them before they have to pass an appropriations bill indicating their approval of the main estimates.
Finally, in the few minutes available to me I hope to touch on the question of the various liabilities that the previous government knew to exist but which they chose not to reflect in those main estimates tabled last February. In short, when the House leader of the opposition asks me whether I approve the main estimates, I have to say they can only be approved in the context of the four other elements that I have indicated. To say otherwise would have been nothing short of making a representation to this House.
Let me go further. As I have said, I welcome the opportunity to make it clear that I am recommending to the House, in the context that I have indicated, that they pass these estimates, the supplementary estimates I have tabled and those I will table in the future which, taken together, and I emphasize this, will represent this government's expenditure plans.

The situation faced by this government with respect to managing expenditures for the current fiscal year is a difficult one. We inherited a set of programs operating in full flight, if you like, on the basis of the spending authorities planned by the previous government, both in the estimates tabled last February and in the subsequent decision of that government. I emphasize that Parliament never approved those spending plans. It was dissolved on March 26 before approving interim supply. Consequently, government operations have been funded through the authority of special Governor General warrants.
This government, in addition to developing our own spending plans in some detail, had to decide on the most responsible method for obtaining parliamentary authority for the funds required to keep the government operating in the current year. One alternative was to develop, print and table in Parliament a completely new set of estimates and to throw the previous blue book away. We are a government of restraint and to have done that would have clearly been a very expensive and time-consuming exercise. The time required was much better spent, in our opinion, on developing the means and on beginning to make the necessary decisions as to how to restrict and redirect spending in 1979-80 and future years.
Consequently we chose the other alternative. We chose to table the estimates in the same form as the previous government. This enabled government operations to proceed as smoothly as possible, avoided the unnecessary cost of printing a revised book, and gave us time to begin to initiate action to control spending. However, I tabled the estimates with the clear understanding that they do not, in isolation, represent precisely how this government plans to spend public funds. The government does not intend to utilize every authority in the estimates to the precise level indicated in the estimates. We will in fact be revising the spending plans represented by the estimates by freezing some funds to be approved in the estimates and will either let those funds lapse or seek parliamentary authority through supplementary estimates for alternative spending.
Hon. members are well aware of some actions already taken by the government to alter the spending plan represented by the estimates. The level of authorized person years for 197980, for which salary and other funds are included in the estimates, has been reduced by about 2 per cent, with a targeted total reduction of 5,000 person years. The associated funds in the estimates will be frozen. A moratorium on all discretionary spending was imposed on departments and agencies from June 8 to October 15. This will result in more funds in the estimates lapsing unspent at the end of the year or being available to offset new spending requirements more consistent with the priorities of this government, as may be approved by Parliament in supplementary estimates.
So you can see, Mr. Speaker, that under the very difficult circumstances imposed by the fact that no estimates were approved before the fiscal year began, the government has chosen the most responsible way of obtaining parliamentary authority for the expenditure of public funds.
October 19, 1979

The technical matter on the tabling of estimates raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) draws attention to a very serious issue which 1 believe it is my responsibility to ensure is fully understood by this House. That issue, Mr. Speaker, is the very adequacy and validity of the over-all spending plan for 1979-80 announced by the previous government when the estimates were tabled last February. At that time the previous government assured this House that the ceiling on total outlays of the government would be $52.6 billion. "Outlays", which was the word they used, included all budgetary expenditures as well as government loans, investments and advances.
I believe there are two very serious criticisms of the plan presented to Parliament, Mr. Speaker. First, it was not an adequate disclosure and proper representation of real spending by the federal government. Second, even if one were to ignore for a moment the very limited range of government activity to which the so-called "outlays" figure applies, the $52.6 billion ceiling was not at all a realisitic figure in light of subsequent actions of that government and the economic situation that they knew to exist.
I would like to deal first with the issue of disclosure. There are three main shortcomings in the previous government's spending plan with respect to the need for full disclosure to Parliament. First, there was absolutely no indication of the level or nature of so-called "tax expenditures". These are provisions in the tax system which result in loss of revenue to the government; for example, the child tax credit and capital cost allowances for businesses. They may be just as important as direct government spending in determining the over-all level and effectiveness of government action in a given policy area. Without some effort by the government at disclosing tax expenditures, the provisions themselves are unlikely to be publicly debated and re-evaluated and it is impossible to assess the true level and effectiveness of government financial involvement.
In this connection, if time would permit, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from the statement made in this House by the then president of the Treasury Board to show how unfair was that statement last February when he initially tabled his main estimates. But let me go on.
My second point is that the previous government did not relate to its $52.6 billion spending plan borrowing by some Crown corporations with the implied guarantee of the government. Under the authority of their governing legislation, some Crown corporations, such as the Export Development Corporation, may borrow funds on the private market rather than from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. These private sector borrowings still represent a contingent liability of the Government of Canada in the order of several billion dollars which are not shown in the estimates or included in "outlays" as defined by the former government.
The third shortcoming of the former government's plan with respect to Parliament's need for full disclosure is related to
The Address-Mr. Stevens
accounting practices. Over a period of many years certain government expenditures were recorded as loans, investments and advances and, therefore, as assets on the books of Canada, when in fact no realizable asset had been created. The result was to distort the apparent net debt of the country.
With respect to the first two items, tax expenditures and off-budget financing, I am not suggesting that they are necessarily inappropriate or improper. Indeed, in many cases they may be thoroughly justified. What 1 am suggesting is that the government has a responsibility to make every effort to ensure that government activities of this type are fully disclosed to Parliament. Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that as the current President of the Treasury Board they will be disclosed from my office in future. If they were not to be disclosed. Parliament could no longer properly evaluate the government's performance or the true Financial impact of government policy.
I say this in full recognition of the fact that, for example, there are some very difficult problems in defining and measuring tax expenditures.
But that is no excuse for doing nothing. In the United States, tax expenditure figures have been published as required by the congressional budget act since 1976. Why should we in Canada say it is impossible? This government has every intention of developing the means of making the maximum diclosure of tax expenditures and obligations created by certain Crown corporation borrowing in association with the direct expenditure plan.
The actions of the former government provide a perfect example of the difficulty of assessing government actions in the absence of such information. They tabled their $52.6 billion spending plan as a model of restraint because of the 8.9 per cent increase it showed over the spending total of the previous year. In the process, however, they had converted certain outlays into tax expenditures for 1979-80. The conversion of child benefits to tax credits with reduced family allowance payments artificially reduced the year to year growth rate in spending as defined by "outlays" because it cost about $650 million in lost revenue.
With respect to accounting practices, the government has already taken action by way of a bill, which received first reading today, to adjust the accounts of Canada. That bill contains clauses which, if passed, will correct several accounting issues and, in particular, two outstanding anomalies which have been contained in estimates of prior years. The first concerns the account known as the airports revolving fund, which at last count amounted to about $650 million and covered the operating and capital expenditures of no fewer than 22 of our national airports, despite which it is classified within the non-budgetary section of the annual estimates presentation. 1 have spoken about this matter before, Mr. Speaker, and I am happy to say that in the future such expenditures will be classified as budgetary in the same way as similar expenditures which are made under the air transportation program.

The Address-Mr. Stevens

speechtext:
At the time this matter came up last March, Your Honour will recall that we, then in opposition, took great exception to some of the steps which were being taken between March 31 last year and April 1 this year. At that time 1 said the present administration was misrepresenting the financial position of the Government of Canada in a desperate attempt to camouflage the actual trends of federal spending and the deficit. Were it not for the fact that taxpayers' money was involved, I went on to say, the bizarre accounting practices of the administration would be worthy of an April Fool's Day joke; but there was nothing funny about what amounts to a loss of $650 million. 1 pointed out that, in effect, the government had put the loan into what it called suspension; they did not want to write it off. 1 make it clear that they did not want to write it off because, if they did, they could no longer show the figure they wished to show in relation to restraint.
I went on to point out that the date of the suspension of the loan is significant-April 1, the start of the new federal fiscal year. This meant that the procedure would not appear in the federal accounts for some time and would probably not be criticized by the Auditor General until the fiscal 1980 report was released in the fall of the subsequent year. Real restraint in federal spending, 1 said at that time, would not be achieved by wizardry in accounting. I added;
As long as government prefers restraint on paper to restraint in fact, none of the tough decisions on real spending restraint can be taken. Until those decisions are taken, Canada will drift ever closer to economic chaos and national bankruptcy.
On taking over as President of the Treasury Board, I found that what I had indicated as critic at that time was exactly what had transpired. Imagine the absolute audacity of the opposition House leader standing up and asking me whether, as President of the Treasury Board, 1 now approve of those estimates, which included the April 1 wizardry to which 1 have just referred!
The second situation which the bill to which I have referred will correct is the manner in which the government's share of the unemployment insurance program has been presented each year in the estimates. Although this has been shown quite properly as a budgetary expenditure, it has always been shown in arrears, the amount in the estimates representing the government's cost only up to the end of the last calendar year. To correct this anomaly and place this account on a current fiscal year basis will require an adjustment in the accounts of Canada in the order of $2.7 billion. That, Mr. Speaker, is what the House should be aware of with respect to the lack of disclosure in the previous government's spending plans.
My second major criticism is that the ceiling of $52.6 billion which the government did place on the narrowly defined outlays portion of its activity was completely unrealistic given its subsequent actions and the economic situation. The $52.6 billion total included main estimates plus $1.35 billion in reserves. When we first had a look at the books after the election, almost exactly one half of those reserves was exhausted. That was $670 million gone in the first two months of the year. More than $115 million of the expenditure cuts announced the previous August had been reinstated after the

estimates were tabled. The figures published in estimates for some programs, such as equalization, were dependent on passage of legislation which to this date has never been passed. Additional costs of several hundred million dollars will result if this legislation cannot be passed this year, and even now we sense that the present opposition is obstructing the progress of this House.

There had been very large overruns in some existing programs, such as payments to VIA Rail, and some decisions had been taken, such as enrichment of the Canadian home insulation program, which would cause charges against reserves at a later date. CHIP alone will cost at least $100 million more than what was shown in the estimates tabled in this House last February. Some non-discretionary increases in major statutory programs had occurred, but the majority of the charges against the reserves had been of a discretionary nature.
That left this government in an untenable position. After two months into the year only half the reserves within the $52.6 billion ceiling were left, and the really major cost increases, such as the oil import compensation program due to huge OPEC price increases, still had to be accommodated somehow.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the difficulties experienced with the tabling of estimates result from the inadequate and unrealistic nature of the spending plan announced by the previous government. That plan did not provide adequate information to Parliament. It also included a figure for total outlays which is unrealistic in light of subsequent action by that government in the economic circumstances.
Nevertheless, 1 am recommending, as I have said, that the House approve the authorities reflected in these estimates, because we have concluded that it is the best means of ensuring an orderly transition to the spending plans of the new government without undue interruption of public services and government operations.
What 1 wish to make clear, however, is that I am not assuming responsibility for the expenditure policies of the previous government which gave rise to the need for these funds to be provided by the House. The policies of this government will be reflected in future supplementary estimates and in new legislation, such as the bill covering adjustments to the accounts of Canada and the forthcoming Crown corporations bill. In addition, as we know, shortly there will be a budget brought in by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie).
In short, it is a long, tangled story which I know the previous government, now the official opposition, only wish could be dropped or obliterated from the records of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my first speech in the House of Commons
October 19, 1979

on a personal note by dedicating my words to the memory of my youngest brother, Robert James Blaikie, who worked very hard on the Winnipeg-Birds Hill NDP sign crew during the spring election campaign but who did not live to see me take my seat in this House because he was struck down by a truck, through no fault of his own, while riding his motorcycle home from the beach last summer.
But, more importantly, in the final analysis it is to the future of all the little brothers and sisters of the world, born and yet to be born, that 1 wish to address my remarks this afternoon. Those who survive may yet be the unlucky ones.
1 understand the tradition of Parliament to be that 1 should initially say something about the riding which I represent, and this I am glad to do. The riding of Winnipeg-Birds Hill is a new riding comprising in part the southern and urban portion of the old federal riding of Selkirk and the town of Transcona, formerly a part of the federal riding of St. Boniface. 1 come from Transcona, 1 am the first person born and raised in Transcona to sit in this House, and for that privilege I thank all the people of Winnipeg-Birds Hill who supported me on May 22 as well as those in Winnipeg-Birds Hill who worked so hard during the election compaign for the NDP.
Winnipeg-Birds Hill is a fairly large and fairly typical urban area throughout most of its parts, with the exception of its northern edge, which is still, and hopefully will continue to be, given over to market gardening and a more rural lifestyle. It is a riding of hardworking people who are paying the bill for this country while corporations and those who run them hide from giving their fair share through perceiving tax loopholes and tax shelters as an opportunity for virtue rather than as the temptation to vice which they in fact are.
The largest single employer in Winnipeg-Birds Hill is the largest single employer in all of Winnipeg, and that is Canadian National Railways, at whose Transcona main repair shops and Symington Yard work many of the people of Winnipeg-Birds Hill. 1 worked there myself as a labourer during summers-and sometimes during the winters as well-while going to university from 1969 to 1974.
It has often been thought and, more recently, said by those who lack foresight and/or by those who have a vested financial interest in highways and related industries that the railroad is on its way out, particularly passenger rail. How anything like that could be said in full knowledge of the energy crisis and in full knowledge of the complete and total supremacy of rail transport over highway transport when it comes to concern about energy is beyond me.
Let me serve notice that any government which wishes to convince me and my constituents in Winnipeg-Birds Hill that it is serious about energy conservation will have to show the wisdom to invest large amounts of money in the modernization and marketing of rail transport in Canada. Nevertheless, one can only be pessimistic about this in view of this government's conceptual inability to distinguish between short-term government spending and long-term government investment, which produces assets and the economic infrastructure which benefits generations to come. No greater example of this kind of
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
conceptual blindness could have been given to us this afternoon than the speech made by the previous speaker.
With respect to passenger rail in particular, this government ought to seek changes in the situation of VIA Rail, the institution set up by the former Liberal government. It appears to preside over the disappearance rather than the revival of passenger rail in Canada. Between old equipment, infrequent service to many areas and collaboration to keep the price of bus travel below the price of passenger rail, there is little to be optimistic about in this area of concern. Just the other day the announcement of the decision to have passengers change trains in Winnipeg late at night could hardly be interpreted as anything but an attack on passenger rail in this country.
The distinction between the short-term and inadequate conceptual framework of this government concerning spending and a longer term, more substantial political vision brings me to the point in my speech where I wish to speak on a broader philosophical level about how this government and the world view which it represents is leading us down the road to destruction. Fundamentally, of course, it is the same road down which the previous government was leading us. The difference is that the former government was leading us there out of cowardice and out of fear to stand up and say that this is the wrong road, whereas this government will lead us there with zeal and a naivete about the world which would be laughable if it were not so tragic. It is hard to know which government is the more to be pitied.
Allow me to elaborate on the error of the direction in which this government so proudly and self-righteously is leading the Canadian people. For many years now, indeed for those centuries that have passed since the beginning of the industrial revolution, the western world, particularly North America, has been guided more or less by what is properly known as Liberal economic doctrine, or the doctrine of the marketplace, as the final adjudicator of what will happen for the good and what will not.
Under this system, there is no question that there has been an incredible increase in the material well-being of a large portion of the world, and thus the accolades for free enterprise that we so often hear from members across the way, not to mention members to the right of our caucus-and, make no mistake, they are where they belong, to the right of us, despite the last minute and hypocritical moans of compassion for the oppressed that we have been treated to this last week or so.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
But this economic growth that the champions of free enterprise are so fond of citing did not happen in a vacuum. It happened at the same time as whole new continents were conquered by the west and technologies improved and developed for the extraction, refinement and secondary manufacturing of resources.
All this growth was had at great cost in human life and
basic human justice. Formerly independent countries were

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
subjected to colonial rule; aboriginal peoples and their cultures were held in contempt and destroyed; traditional and renewable resource economics were dislocated for the profit of the powerful, and many within the powerful industrial nations themselves were reduced to starvation and the slavery of necessity as they streamed into the factories to try to eke out a living.
This was capitalism at its worse, the kind of capitalism we have now exported to the Third World. At home, however, the development of unions at no small cost in human suffering, the development of orderly marketing in some areas, either through government control or private sector monopoly, and the development of government regulation and government ownership for the public interest, have blunted the effects of raw competition and profit seeking.
At the same time, we have seen the development of large multinational corporations whose power overshawdows that of most nations of the world and who are able to blackmail and ruin national economies at will. We have seen the slowing down of the western world economically as we come to the limits of our ability to dominate the planet, not just for economic reasons, but also for environmental and physical reasons as pollution increases and resources are depleted. We have been able to observe that, in spite of all the wind which passes on the other side about opportunity and progress, hundreds of thousands of Canadians live without work, without a decent standard of living, without hope for a better life. Finally, at the same time we have seen a gradual erosion of community life, of family life and of meaning. Life is meaningless for so many people. We produce and consume, we keep the economy going, we are told to be good consumers. We exist for the sake of the economy. I am reminded of Tommy Douglas' excellent interpretation of the biblical teaching that the economy is made for man, not the man for economy.
This short historical sketch raises three questions: the question of power, that of limit, and that of meaning. All of them are related to the future.
On the question of power, it is customary to hear conversations about big government, big business, and big labour, with much emphasis on increasing power of government. I am no promoter of bureaucracy but when it comes to a choice between big government and big business-because in this country there is no such thing as big labour-let me say why I come down on the side of government. It is not a question of bigness versus smallness, or government versus the individual. All this talk about the individual and individual freedom as justification for letting large corporations do what they want is evidence of complete blindness to reality on the part of some and of cheap political jingoism on the part of others. One would like to think that it is the leaders who are the jingoists and the followers who are the dupes, but listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) one suspects it is the other way around.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Corporations are not individuals by any twist of the imagination, and for that matter individuals are not

individuals in the way we usually hear this word used by Liberals and Conservatives. We have our being in relation to others and we try to be rugged individuals at our peril and to the peril of the world.
I was talking about power, Mr. Speaker. Power must be made accountable, and if the choice is not between big and small but rather who is going to be big until we can decentralize our lives a bit more through the development of technologies which require less centralization, then, given this choice, 1 say that there must be more government involvement, not less. So long as we continue to have and continue to improve the democratic nature of governments so that power is more and more accountable, this will be a good thing, not a bad thing.
The alternative to this reallocation of power so as to make it more accountable to the democratic process is to continue to let very important decisions be made privately according to the criteria of maximum profit instead of public justice and survival of the human prospect. The talk on the other side about returning control to individual Canadians through privatization is a farce, a false description of the reality of allowing a few Canadians, and even more non-Canadians, through foreign ownership, to control the rest of us, those of us who cannot afford to pretend that we control something by owning even a few shares in a corporation, and for that matter may not be interested in earning a living through investment but rather through hard work in the productive or service sector of our society.
Power is to be mistrusted because it can be, and mostly is, corrupted by the vanity of human kind, expressed in control, and by a selfishness of human kind expressed through exploitation. So even the power of democratic governments must be held in constant check by a vigilant and informed citizenry. 1 have no illusions about the negative aspect of government, but, nonetheless, government is a more appropriate avenue of accountability than the vain hope that corporations, imprisoned as they are by the structures of profit maximization and protected by governments which think it their responsibility to give them a free hand, can ever really act substantially and in a prolonged way for the benefit of all, and particularly of those who inhabit the future.
Next to the question of power there is the question of limit, or of realizing the limits within which we act as humans in a finite universe which exists not just for our sake but for its own sake, something declared to be valuable by the creator, independent of human existence. For too long our relationship to nature has been one of domination, of viewing it as merely an instrument of our own self-interest. This has been true, to a greater or lesser extent, of all major western ideological streams, including the democratic socialist tradition. On this account, we are all in need of repentance. But this error has been compounded in many so-called advanced countries by the addition of competitive economics to the tragedy.
So we have seen the following, Mr. Speaker. Valuable resources have been depleted for no other reason than that it was profitable to sell them as fast as could be to as many as could be. When I think of all the gas and oil that would yet be
October 19, 1979

available for important uses and for future development of underdeveloped as opposed to overdeveloped areas, I get sick with anger in the knowledge that this was done for no other reason than to increase the global profit margins of a few large corporations, which then had the nerve to pay little or no tax to societies whose future they so endanger.
When I think of depleted fish stocks, of soil paved over or spoiled by overfertilization for short-term yields, or of all the valuable forest that goes into packaging and bagging hamburgers that are already wrapped, all for the sake of what is innocently called marketing, I become fearful at just what kind of judgment history reserves for such a society.
Then there is the problem of pollution, that other great hallmark of the system with which members opposite are so fascinated. River after river-the English-Wabigoon river system, for instance-lake after lake-Lake Erie is the first thing that comes to mind-and place after place-one can hardly help thinking of the Sudbury basin-fouled by the great benefactors of mankind who, for all their user-pay rhetoric, when it comes to health care and other human rights have been consistently unwilling to pay the full cost of their economic activities.
The full environmental, not to mention social, costs of traditional economic development are enormous, and we have just begun to pay them. Indeed, the sons will have to pay for the sins of the fathers. Let the corporate sector bear the full cost of their activities, and let them be silent for once on the government spending required to remedy their social and environmental sins. The gleam in their own eye is so big that they are tripping over themselves with self-righteous blindness.
We live in a finite universe. What this means, among other things, is that if we continue to remain committed to an economic system which requires infinite growth to be healthy, then we are committed to a logical fallacy in theory and disaster in practice. What is worse is that this government would have us uncritically rededicate ourselves to this undesirable end, when I can think of a no more fundamentally wrong direction in which to go. Rather, we must learn to seek ways of organizing our economic life so that we do not have to grow all the time, so that everyone has enough, and so that social and environmental considerations may be given priority-a planned economy. The CCF called for it in 1933, and the need for it is relevant today in ways that J. S. Woodsworth probably could not have imagined.
Economic growth is not the solution to things that it is thought to be, both because it does not guarantee justice and because it does not fulfil the need for meaning in life. I do not say this self-righteously. I am conscious of the fact that governments of the left have not always been environmentally responsible, and that they too have been too uncritical of economic growth. What I do submit is that these errors are not inherent, are not built into the very concept of society which, for instance, we in the New Democratic Party advocate. We have the conceptual tools, and I believe also the character, to
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
face up to these problems of limit because we are not bound within the ideological prison that members opposite find themselves in, which I submit makes them enemies of the future whether they know it or not, and for the sharper among them, whether they like it or not.
The question of meaning is the third problem which I raise concerning the direction in which this government would lead us. It is the most ironic problem of all three. As I listened over the last eight days to the speeches of the members opposite, the conviction grew in me that these men and women are their own worst enemies. They lament and they wail about the erosion of values, of hard work, of family ties, of community consciousness, of duty, and somehow imagine that this is the result of a socialist plot. It is their world view that has been running the world for the last few centuries, not ours. It is their world view that has been running the country since its inception, not ours. The failure of the system to hold the community together is their failure and no one else's. It is their failure because the one value they hold above all others is the value of economic freedom, the freedom to make a buck wherever and whenever one can and the corresponding emphasis on material wealth as the measure of a person's worth, and indeed the measure of a country's worth. It is this very value inculcated from day one, and reinforced over and over again by advertising and by Tory pamphlets, that is eating away at all the other things they hold dear.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), who is not present today, spoke last week quite eloquently about the disappearance of good agricultural land. Yet if asked to support land use planning, even if it went against the economic freedom of land developers, my money is on the prediction that he would back down. It is not socialists who have allowed the haphazard and unplanned development of our urban areas to happen; it is city councils all over this country of the same mentality as this government. Winnipeg city council is one of the worst examples of a so-called non-partisan government whose allegiance to developers knows no shame.
I have heard members opposite lament the destruction of community spirit. The Prime Minister in particular likes to go on about the value of small community life. I ask them: Who is destroying the family farm and small businesses all over this country? Not the socialists but the economics of growing multinational control, of agribusiness, and of chain stores. It was NDP provincial governments which tried through stay-options and land lease programs to maintain rural life in Canada. We are the true conservatives. We are the ones who would intervene to conserve what is valuable and good about Canadian life, rather than abandoning it to the whim and self-interest of the economically powerful in the name of this specious freedom which serves no one but the powerful themselves.
What we have before us are a sort of primitive nineteenth century classical Liberals who represent the latest revolt of the powerful against what little progress in social justice has been accomplished already. As for the Liberal party, an attempt to locate it ideologically would require that one have in one's

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
hand the latest Gallup poll. Pragmatism is the name given to the ideology of the Liberals. Pragmatism is the name given to this lack of principle and power, and power only is the name of the ideology that the Liberal party has, in spite of its hypocritical criticisms of the government and the NDP for being ideological. It is impossible not to have an ideology. Theirs is the most despicable of all because they refuse to admit it, lest they would have to defend it, of course.
Human life cannot much longer bear the suffering which Adam Smith's invisible hand, indeed non-existent hand, has visited upon the world until now, and the disaster that it will visit upon the world should it continue to be mistakenly perceived to be there. It is clearly not the case that the best interests of all are served by allowing and encouraging everyone as individuals to pursue their own self-interest. This would be to build a house on sand, a house that will blow over as the strong winds of economic reality blow on it and various individuals, groups, or provinces scramble to protect their share of a shrinking pie, a scramble that is called "good business" when engaged in by the powerful and called "living beyond our means" when engaged in by the powerless.
