I must confess a certain sympathy for the latter category because it is my belief that when there is scarcity, it is immoral for those who are well off to decide that their standard of living is the one thing which must be protected above all else and restraint imposed on everyone else. This is the time when the commitment of the Canadian establishment to social justice is being tested and found wanting.
We must build our country not out of dreams of riches, of opening up new frontiers and all the other stuff the Prime Minister likes to go on about, but on the rock of human community expressed in the equal sharing of our country's wealth with each other and with the world. We must build it on the rock of respect for the non-human environment and the future, expressed in an economic system which does not demand growth yet which permits appropriate growth in underdeveloped areas. We must build it on the rock of democratic accountability of power, so that important decisions affecting society and its future are made in the public rather than the private sector. Only in this way will we be able to negotiate a future which we can look forward to.
In other words, to quote W. H. Auden, "We must love one another or die . The world is too small now and human actions too significant and powerful to be placed at the disposal of the marketplace and the values it represents. We have a crisis of values, but it is not the crisis that members opposite think it is.
It is not only that we have seen the erosion of traditional values; we have at least one traditional value, the value placed on our economic system, which has led to the present crisis. The sooner it is dumped, the sooner we will be able to restore and refurbish those values, the passing of which is appropriately lamented.
We must love one another or die, not just through charity or the new routine platitudes of Conservatives about the volun-

tary sector in social services, but as the very structures of our economy, our politics, and life together as a people among other peoples comes to reflect the theological truth that, whether it fits our ideological fantasies or not, we are brothers and sisters, children of the same God who intended that we live in fellowship rather than in competition with each other, and in fellowship with Him and creation.
We have before us in this century, and particularly at this juncture, the choice between life and death, between love and continued separation from each other. We have chosen death so many times before. How long before our choices are irreversible, before we gain the whole world and lose our souls?
I have heard members opposite disparage comments like mine as so much doom crying and lack of confidence in the Canadian people. But my idea of responsible leadership is not to be a cheerleader. I am reminded of the distinction between false prophecy and true prophecy which we find in the dispute between Jeremiah and Hananiah in the Book of Jeremiah. Those who prophesy peace, who would heal the wounds of the people lightly, who are afraid to be anything but optimistic and superficial, are not to be trusted. They would save us not by repentance or change, but by more of the same.
We must amend our ways and our doings. There is no salvation in pious phrases about reduction in government spending. It is to the amending of our ways and our doings that my work in this Parliament will be directed. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by joining with members on both sides of the House in offering my congratulations to the hon. member for Sudbury
The Address-Mr. Jupp
(Mr. Jerome) on the occasion of his re-election as Speaker of this House.
This might be an appropriate time to bring to the attention of the House a message that was conveyed to me as a new member of Parliament as I met with electors in the longest election campaign in Canadian history. In my case it was a campaign which lasted for 14 months. Indeed, I must express my appreciation to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau), the former prime minister. It was because of his reluctance to call the election in the spring of 1978 at the end of the normal mandate of the last Parliament that 1 was able to visit so many electors throughout Mississauga North and thus be elected to Parliament. Were the Leader of the Opposition in his seat today, 1 would say to him that had he followed his own instincts and not listened to the bad advice of his bad advisers, I would not be here in this Parliament and he would likely not be on that side of the House.
My message, however, is less one of consoling hindsight to the official opposition than it is to the members on both sides of the House, particularly those who sat in the last Parliament. This institution is not held in high regard by Canadians. Indeed, some view Parliament as the only institution in the country that is run by the inmates themselves. During the division bells last week one young visitor to the House asked his friend what the noise was all about. His friend replied that he did not know, but maybe it was because one of the members escaped!
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I was given the distinct impression, in my months of house to house visiting prior to the official election call, that Canadians question the relevance of much of what goes on in the House. The first issue of Parliamentary Government, a journal which I would commend to all Canadians seriously interested in the integrity of Parliament, addresses the question in an article on "Public Opinion: Why Don't Canadians Trust Their Representatives?" and I quote:
The behaviour of members may appear rowdy, frivolous, and unworthy of the seriousness of the matters under discussion. Where increased public understanding is the goal, there are some doubts about the ability of television to contribute to this understanding under the present broadcasting format.
I do have hope for improvement, Mr. Speaker, because of the decorum of the new members on both sides of this House. My hope is that this Thirty-first Parliament will be seen as a turning point in respect of this House and the great tradition for which it stands. Let us refrain from the catcalls, the posturing, and the irrelevance that have brought disrepute to this great democratic institution, and dedicate our presence to a serious discussion of the public issues.
On this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in tribute to the late Right Honourable John George Diefenbaker. Above all, Mr. Diefenbaker was a man who loved Parliament and the historical traditions for which it stood. We can honour his memory in no greater way than by dedicating ourselves to respecting and preserving those laws, traditions and institutions which history has proven to be the basic ingredients of any lasting progress.

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Jupp
Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to be the practice of new members to say a few words about the constituency which sent them to this House. I rather suspect that, with the exception of Ottawa Centre in which the Houses of Parliament are located, more members have visited Mississauga North than any other riding in the country. This is because it is the home of the Toronto international airport. Mississauga North is the second most populous constituency in Canada. It contains the communities of Streetsville, Malton, and Cooksville, which are over a hundred years old, as well as the very new communities of Erin Mills, Meadowvale, Rockwood, and Mississauga Valleys. Its diversity is reflected in the densely populated Dixie-Bloor area, where I reside, while a few miles away abound the pastures of over 100 farms. As well it includes the picturesque communities of Applewood Acres, Applewood Hills, Apple-wood Heights, Fleetwood Village, and the Credit Woodlands.
It is very much a multicultural constituency, comprising citizens of over 80 countries, the majority of whom are of neither Anglo-Saxon nor French origin. I am grateful for the confidence they have placed in me as their representative in this Parliament, and pledge myself to work with you on their behalf to address the serious problems confronting our great country.
I felt compelled to enter public life because of a profound concern for the direction the previous government was leading this country. I became convinced that nothing short of a defeat of that government was necessary if Canada was going to chart out a new course and avoid the disaster that would surely come to this nation had the Canadian people voted otherwise last spring.
In the past decade, the government's share of Canada's gross national product has grown from 33.7 per cent to 41.1 per cent. What is the significance of these comparative ratios to the average Canadian? In terms of impact on our everyday lives, probably very little. However, when these figures are projected into the future they become ominous indeed. They really tell us of the extent to which government-all governments, federal, provincial, and municipal-are shaping and controlling the destiny of our political economy. It has been argued that once government controls more than 40 per cent of a nation's production the trend becomes irreversible-that the nation is on a course to inevitable state control of the means of production and distribution of all goods and services.
We have never had a referendum or bill repealing economic freedom, and there is little evidence of a consensus for a national goal of collectivism. Nevertheless, we are drifting from a society that once valued thrift, initiative, and reward for effort into one where governments are borrowing from the future to meet rising expectations which they have helped to fuel.
Almost a quarter of what the federal government now spends comes not from taxes or general revenues but by borrowing from capital markets or printing new money. In the past decade, Canadians have seen the rise of a powerful

political system. The federal public service, excluding military and Crown corporation personnel, has grown from 237,000 to 317,000, an increase of 34 per cent. The operating costs of the federal government have quadrupled, and federal spending has quintupled. In the same ten-year period, taxes paid per person have increased three and three-quarter times.
It is noteworthy that if, during the period of controls, the federal government had heeded the same guidelines for restraint as they set out for the rest of us, federal expenditures would be $3.3 billion lower than they stand at present. Long before the introduction of controls which had the effect of transferring critical management decisions from the private sector to the government, there was clear evidence of a trend to turn to government as the ultimate determinant in what has been labelled the "political bargaining arena".
My concern, one which I hope goes beyond partisan considerations, is that this drift toward a larger state role will result in a boring and sterile society from which excellence, and perhaps freedom, too, will vanish. History tells us that no society can remain free in terms of civil rights or the political process when its people have transferred all significant powers to its government. It is a concern which goes beyond the prospects for our economic system to the future of Canadian society.
Civilization moves forward through ideas. The dynamics of progress of any country are essentially the dynamics of ideas- the extent to which the nation is effecitively able to develop and utilize its creative power and its human talents. The way in which ideas emerge into the mainstream of the social, cultural, political, and economic life of a nation has a great deal to do with its progress and destiny. My point is that the processes of idea creation, of national planning, of alternative futures exploration, of resource deployment and priority-setting-all of the basic processes which ultimately determine the kind of society in which future generations will live-seem to have been turned over to government. We have come to expect from government the development of the grand design because we have turned over to it the responsibility for managing, financing, and challenging social change. We must now recognize that governments are not supremely wise and infinitely perfect and that, like all human institutions, they never will be. Thus, only disaster can result when a country's ideas, knowledge, and intellectualism become subservient to government.
The time is ripe for the emergence of new approaches to social, political, and economic problems. We are entering an era when Canada and the western industrialized nations must turn to new avenues of creative power for civilization's advance. To strain all this creative power through the funnel of power politics and bureaucratic compression would defeat the very purpose of such a vital endeavour. The result would be a political monotheism that fossilizes all human progress. Our task must be to seek out the kind of initiatives which are required to bring about a rebirth of a creative free society in a dramatically new context. We must begin the creative adventure in the quest for larger truths, a higher order of morality, responsible philosophical perception, and visionary leadership.
October 19, 1979

I am not suggesting we should attempt to drive government back to its passive role of half a century ago. That is neither desirable nor possible. However, there must surely be some human alternative to the notion that all we really need to solve our problems is simply another scoop of government.
1 believe there is deep concern about society's drift and the dearth of renewing ideas which comes from creeping statism. What is urgently needed before we reach the point of no return is an intelligent dialogue and debate on the sickness of an overgoverned society. Canadians are receptive to constructive proposals grounded in the public interest that promise any possible rational recovery from the malaise with which we are afflicted. The problems confronting our social institutions present seemingly insurmountable dilemmas. I am confident, however, that they can be solved in a creative society in which our citizens are encouraged to utilize their political will and optimal intelligence.
Mr. Speaker, permit me to set out a few of these ideas which I submit in the hope that they may be considered to be worthy of thought as a disciplined intellectual, if not constitutional, framework for new directions to Canada's political economy.
First, to reverse the trend to increasing government control of our private institutions, we might permit citizens to directly allocate up to $100 of their income taxes to non-profit, voluntary agencies. Organizations such as those engaged in education, recreation, sports, health, medical research, and the arts would benefit, as well as newly created agencies with new hope for financial viability. The consequences would be a reduced dependency on government, reversing the drift to state control which threatens the dynamism of a free pluralistic society, and shifting the locus of funding power from government to the hearts, minds, and purses of individual Canadians. This could have the effect of unleashing a productive synergy through the creation of new associations for the study of such apparently insoluble problems as inflation, unemployment, industrial strife, crime, poverty, and war, as well as centres for the study of alternative energy resources and alternative futures research.
Second, each Parliament should be required to balance its budget for the life of that Parliament. The last Parliament added more than $30 billion to the public debt, with interest charges more than doubling. Altering this course is both a moral and an economic imperative. We must now give thought to making it a political imperative. Governments must not be allowed to buy power by stealing from the future. To pay for what we want today, as a society, we must have the moral courage to tax our citizens and to raise the funds necessary to meet those wants. Instead of belittling the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) in the hope of political advantage, we should lend him our full moral and political support. I say to both the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) that, notwithstanding the terrible legacy of the previous decade, the people of Canada will stand behind them in the tough decisions they will have to make.
The Address-Mr. Jupp
As a nation we are confronted with three real choices when it comes to government spending: First, a drastic reduction in expenditures, including cuts in programs which none of us really want to see cut; second, a major increase in revenues, largely through increased taxation, or; third, national bankruptcy. The mindless spending of the previous administration has had the effect of fueling inflation, debasing our currency, and robbing our citizens of their savings. It is the very difficult task of this administration to restore common sense to government spending, notwithstanding the opportunistic posturing of some hon. members opposite.
Third, the size of the bureaucracy should be reduced by at least 60,000, not including Crown corporations. It should then be limited according to our population growth. The centralized federal bureaucracy interferes with every aspect of our daily lives. It regulates and directs our business affairs, taps our telephones, opens our mail, misuses our tax returns, invades premises without warrant, and tries individuals in secret courts. Only an alert Parliament, aided by constitutional change, will mitigate such abuses of our liberty.
Fourth, the dates for the calling of general elections should be prescribed, every four years. We should not give prime ministers the right to play games with the electorate, with political parties and with the lives of those who offer themselves for public office. I am not advocating a limitation on parliamentary democracy. The government must at all times retain the confidence of the House of Commons. However, I believe that the calling of elections is too important to be left to the whim of prime ministers or their advisers' interpretations of the latest Gallup poll. These are just a few of the ideas I gathered from my one year of knocking on doors in Mississauga North.
I am heartened by the determination of our new Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) to restore Parliament as a responsible and useful instrument of idea creation, by his frank and open communications with Parliament and the Canadian people, and by his preparedness not just to tolerate but also to encourage dissent as a useful contribution to public policy formation. These are all refreshing signs which lead me to be optimistic about the future of this Parliament, of this government and, indeed, of Canada.
Notwithstanding the legacy of serious fiscal imbalance, of an emasculated Parliament, of inflation, of unemployment, of debt and of confrontation-all of the factors which have contributed to our national malaise-there is hope for this country. I am convinced, however, that if we want to restore some sense of social and economic stability and some sense of nationhood, we must give serious thought to the direction in which we are going. We Canadians, through this Parliament, require a commitment to new national goals.
We have the potential. We have a rich and diversified resource base. We have sophisticated technology which places us in the scientific forefront. We have a high level of personal savings for investment because we are a prudent people. We have some of the best cereal grain-growing lands and forests in

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. McRae
the world. We have an educated work force. We have the potential to become self-sufficient in energy, and we have the blood of a hundred nations flowing through our veins. No other country in the world has more to offer to its people. No other country has all those ingredients. What we lacked in the past was the political will to put those ingredients together.
This is the challenge of this Parliament. This is the challenge of this government. Let us go forward with a zest for achievement, new ideas for nation building, and new ideals for excellence. Let us go forward in the creative adventure of providing new direction to Canada of which we can all be proud.

Mr. Speaker, as is customary, 1 would like first to congratulate the Speaker on his election. Those of us who sat through the Thirtieth Parliament are well aware of the contribution he made to Parliament in terms of increasing its prestige and enlarging its scope and power. Under Mr. Speaker we had the advent of television in the House, and in many ways his support and his working with Parliament have added immeasurably to the prestige of Parliament.
1 congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) for their acceptance and for nominating Mr. Speaker, with the idea that he is the very best person in the House we could possibly find to take care of the needs of this House.
It is customary for new members at the beginning of their speeches to speak about their constituencies, and I would like to do that myself, even though I have been here for two Parliaments, because my constituency, like all our constituencies, changed somewhat in the course of the last election.
The constituency I represented in the past was Fort William, part of the city of Thunder Bay. The constituency has been enlarged and has joined with a part of another constituency. It now includes the community and area around it about 140 miles from Thunder Bay, known as Atikokan. Atikokan is a mining community different from Thunder Bay, which is basically a pulp and paper and manufacturing community.
Unfortunately, in the last year Atikokan has gone through a rather bad transformation. One of the major mines has shut down, and the second mine will be shut down within the next six months or so. However, this community has shown some real fortitude and decided that it is going to continue. Its people have put together many new enterprises, and they are looking forward to the coming on stream of another mine, Bending Lake, in the next two or three years. I will be very pleased to represent the people of that area and to push as hard as I can for the coming on stream of this particular mine. We will be watching things like pipelines and how well the government handles the Foothills and other pipeline deals, which will increase the demand for iron ore and bring on the Bending Lake operation more quickly.
The city of Thunder Bay is Canada's largest grain port and one of the world's largest grain ports, if not the largest. It very

seldom is mentioned in terms of the moving of grain. There was an article recently in the Toronto Star and an editorial in The Globe and Mail about all the difficulties we are having regarding the movement of grain. The articles mentioned rail problems, labour problems and so forth, but in neither of these articles was the city of Thunder Bay mentioned, even though two thirds of all the grain shipped out of this country goes through Thunder Bay, twice as much as Vancouver.
As a matter of fact, I believe it is estimated that we could move all the grain going through Churchill out through Thunder Bay in four days in any given season. The port is grossly under-utilized. We could handle twice as much grain if we had sufficient rail cars. I am concerned about this because Dr. Horner recently suggested that one of the solutions to the problem of grain movement might be to move unit trains to the east coast, bypassing Thunder Bay. Of course this does not make very much sense. In the first place, the major reason grain is not moving the way it should be is that we do not have a sufficient number of rail cars. The railways are not moving grain as they should. If we move grain by unit trains to the east coast we will need three or four times as many rail cars as would be needed to move grain just to Thunder Bay.
The second major point which must be understood is that one of the main reasons Thunder Bay is so efficient is that grain moves from Thunder Bay 2,200 miles to the open sea, or to Sept-Isles. That grain goes out on a ship, the grain is unloaded and iron ore is brought back to Sault Ste. Marie and to some American ports. That is a very major development. It is a very major transportation activity in our country. The efficiency of Thunder Bay depends a great deal on the fact that ships do not come back with empty bottoms. I think a great deal more thought should be given to utilization, and I hope this government will consider greater utilization of the port of Thunder Bay.
Perhaps one of the misconceptions we have is that all grain moving to China, Japan and Asia must go through west coast ports. A very senior official of CPR said to me in a conversation that he is convinced that if the Crowsnest rates were not in place, it would be cheaper to move grain from Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba to Thunder Bay and by ship through the Panama Canal and to Asia than it would be to move it across the Rocky Mountains into Vancouver.
I would like to mention one other point regarding the port of Thunder Bay because I think it is important. We have not had a major labour stoppage or a major strike since 1968. To conclude on this particular point, I should like the House and the government to know that the Thunder Bay operation is very efficient, very cheap, and very under-utilized.
We in opposition have to learn this new role, much the same way as hon. members opposite, having spent many years in oppostion, have to learn the new role of government. There is no doubt about that, and it is a different process either way. I think it behooves us to give the government a bit of a chance, while we are trying to get our act together, to show what it is going to do. We should not be too critical.
October 19, 1979

For many reasons we were not as critical of the government this summer perhaps as we might have been regarding some of the things it did. I still believe they have to work things out, and 1 do not believe it is our job to tear them apart in the first six months or so of the operation. But I am concerned about one major trend-1 am concerned and it worries me-because I think that one of the facts of life about this country is that we are very weak as a federal government.
This is not a strong federation, it is a weak federation. For a long time, under previous governments, power has been gravitating to the provinces. Some of that is desirable, some is necessary, but I think we have made mistakes. 1 think that one of the mistakes of which we can be accused is block funding in one form or another, the transfer of power to the provinces. I do not envy the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie) his job at this point. There is so much transfer of power to the provinces in that area that federal authorities cannot control medicare the way they should be able to control it. 1 think these are some of the mistakes we have made.
I am seriously afraid that this government is continuing this drift, and perhaps even accelerating it. I am concerned when 1 hear the Prime Minister goes to Newfoundland, to British Columbia, and to Nova Scotia and talks about handing away offshore rights. In Newfoundland there is a slightly different constitutional twist to this, but certainly as regards British Columbia and Nova Scotia there is no question about what the constitutional rights are. Offshore resources belong to the people of Canada, to all of Canada. That has clearly been declared by the Supreme Court, and I think it is understood by all. There is nothing wrong with the government of this country making a deal, as we did in the past, and saying, "Okay, we will share these resources, 75 per cent to you, 25 per cent to us." But to say that these will be handed over directly to the provinces is not acceptable.
I am concerned about a series of other things that have happened. I am concerned, for instance-this is a small thing perhaps-about the transfer of Loto Canada, which was Canadian and had some merit, which supported Canadian sports, about its transfer, with considerable loss of revenue to the government. 1 am concerned very much about oil pricing, whether or not this is something that gives one province a very strong advantage over another province. 1 am concerned about the selling, giving away or transferring of Crown corporations to the private sector or, possibly, to the provinces.
1 am especially concerned about PetroCan because that is something for which, from the very beginning, from the time it was first announced by the government, or even before it was announced, I and some of my colleagues here fought very hard. We fought very hard to set this very important piece into the energy policy of this country. In a country where the resources are controlled by the provinces, where the ownership of our resources is so much in the hands of foreign corporations, of multinationals, there is very little left for a federal government to do in the field of energy because we do not have
The Address-Mr. McRae
power. So it is extremely and vitally important that there be an instrument of federal power in terms of energy. Perhaps the most important instrument of federal power, of federal ability to initiate and pursue energy activities in this country, is PetroCan. That is the fundamental reason why it exists, the fundamental reason why we as the government set it up.
I become annoyed when people on my left-just physically on my left, not fundamentally so-grab hold of this issue and say "This is our creation." It is not their creation, it is our creation. We have worked hard for it and we have fought against many members on the other side, including the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), to establish that company. It was done because we needed that fundamental instrument for an energy policy. We needed something to ensure we had an adequate supply of energy for all Canadians, not just for the people in this province or that province.
Members of the government may say they will allow some activities, such as the drilling that has been going on. Last year, in 1978, PetroCan was involved in over 50 per cent of the drilling in the north, and yet it is still the sixth smallest oil company in Canada. I think it was involved in the drilling of 11 out of 13 wells on the east coast, and it was responsible for such things as the Sable Island gas find. These are fundamental to the future of this country at a time when energy shortages are becoming evident to all. So I just do not understand the government that would weaken or destroy this company, that would take the assets, as the leader of the NDP has said, of this country and privatize them, socialize all the liabilities and remove the possibility of the company acting independently, having a decent cash flow and being able to function on its own.
Basically, when you take away Pacific Petroleums, you take away from PetroCan a lot of the technology to function. It will lose its role to be an eye on the industry, an industry which most Canadians do not trust. It is an industry that is not trusted, and yet we have taken away, by this apparent act of the government, the ability to look at the industry and tell us what is happening. The government has made a very major decision and we in the opposition will fight very hard, not to defeat the government so much, but to stop this change. We will fight very hard to ensure that this bill does not go through, that Canada will retain a strong instrument for an energy policy in this country.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about economic policy because I think there is a kind of misconception in the House and in the country that the high interest energy policy of the previous government is the same as the high interest energy policy of this government. I would like to spend a good deal more time on it, but I think I have only about three minutes left. However, 1 would like to make this point very clear.
When we were in power we had an interest rate which disturbed me. There was no question about that. I have had some real doubts about the Keynesian notion that one can

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Darling
manipulate seriously the money supply by the interest rate. I think that is a dead thing. It was functioning for a long time, but I think it is dead now. But there is a fundamental difference between now and then. At that particular time we were following the American interest rates, and there was some point in that. Also at that particular time the difference between the Canadian inflation rate and the Canadian interest rate was approximately 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent. So the net interest was approximately 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent. Roughly that is the situation with the American interest rate today. But the prime rate in Canada now is approximately 13.5 per cent or 14 per cent, and the inflation rate is approximately 9 per cent or 9.5 per cent. So there is about a four or five percentage point difference. The key factor is that the American spread is 1 per cent or 2 per cent and our spread is 4 per cent or 5 per cent. We do not need that kind of spread. We will be arguing very strongly against increasing interest rates further. We will be arguing very strongly for lowering interest rates because of the nature of the spread.
In conclusion, I should like to say that I am watching the government very carefully. 1 am very, very disturbed that we may be giving away what is vital to Canada being able to continue as a nation. I am concerned that the fundamental economic policies of the government are not in tune with the times. We will be watching those particular things during the next one, two or three years.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly it is an honour to have the opportunity this afternoon to participate in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I congratulate the mover and the seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) respectively, for their very articulate and excellent speeches. Congratulations are also in order to the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) on his re-election to the high and respected post of Speaker of the House of Commons. The re-election is a sign of the great trust and high regard which many of us place in his ability to preside over the deliberations of this representative body. Also, may I extend my personal congratulations to the Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House (Mr. McCain) and his colleagues on their appointment to important positions.
I feel honoured to have the opportunity to extend a warm welcome to all of those members who are gracing this chamber for the first time, and a great many members who have made outstanding speeches already. I feel greatly honoured to be back in this august chamber having first come here in 1972, almost seven years ago. I am deeply indebted to the voters of Parry Sound-Muskoka who, through their action, have given me the honour to represent them in the House. I assure the constituents of Parry Sound-Muskoka that their concerns and interests will remain always in the forefront of my decisions.
I would ask for a brief indulgence to pay homage to the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker whose demise has deprived the
(Mr. McRae.]
Parliament of Canada of one of its staunch supporters and participants. While one accepts his passing away with deep regret and sorrow, one cannot help but feel a vacuum in this chamber. The right hon. gentleman's monumental contributions to Canada in numerous forms will long be remembered dearly. What I may utter today will not do justice to the dedicated task of attaining some lofty principles for Canada. However, I wish to register my deep respect for what the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker stood for. I hope many of us will be able to carry on this noble task in various fields and many more must aspire to the ideals for Canada outlined in the long public career of the late right honourable gentleman.
I see nothing more befitting to grace Parliament hill than a statue of the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. I am sure one of the highlights in the visits to Ottawa and Parliament of many tourists and Canadians would be a visit to such a statue. If the excuse for the delay in erecting such a monument is financial, I am certain Canadians will donate generously toward this project. A statue will be the best tribute we can pay to the man who so strongly guarded parliamentary tradition throughout his entire lifetime.
I cannot help but feel that the entire country from coast to coast took in a breath of fresh hope on May 22. The vigour and dynamism of the new government are beginning to provide the kind of leadership the voters had hoped for in the Progressive Conservative government. I highly commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) for his outstanding speech earlier in this debate. He briefly outlined the program of action for Canada which the government expects to pursue. It is a plan which I support. Also I share the vision the Prime Minister has for Canada. We seem to have turned the corner in the matter of federal-provincial relations on to the road of co-operation and understanding. This may be our chance to bridge the rifts of the past. The new Prime Minister has displayed compassion and understanding in his dealings with the many issues confronting our nation today.
Since I represent the picturesque riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka, I am delighted to have read the following in the Speech from the Throne:
In co-operation with the provinces and industry, a national tourism strategy will be developed.
If I recall correctly, this is probably the first time tourism has been given such high recognition at the federal level. This commendable action will give rise to some form of organized approach to resolving some of the difficulties encountered by the tourism industry. It is hard to imagine that such an important industry as tourism has been on the back burner for so long. It is an industry which can help restore balance to our international trade picture. For instance, tourism earned approximately $2 billion in foreign exchange last year. Furthermore, there is every indication tourism is on its way to becoming our leading industry in income, export earnings, and employment by the end of the century. Today tourism is a labour-intensive industry, fortunately absorbing a large segment of the labour force. It employs almost 9 per cent of the
October 19, 1979

Canadian work force, or approximately one million people. Tourism and travel generate an income of $11 billion a year for Canadians. This accounts for 5 per cent of our gross national product.
During the summer a special caucus committee was formed with a mandate to look into various aspects of the tourism industry. The committee heard evidence from representatives of various sectors in the industry. One matter was made abundantly clear, and that is that we should give tourism the higher profile it rightly deserves. In this regard 1 have on many earlier occasions spoken in favour of establishing a secretariat for tourism. Once again 1 voice my concern that the delay in establishing such a secretariat will continue to affect adversely this very important industry.
In the spirit of freedom of expression which the Prime Minister would like to encourage among our ranks, I should like the government to consider setting up a secretariat for tourism at the earliest, and include the responsibility for tourism in the title of the minister. The caucus committee on tourism heard representations from various groups, including Tourism Industry Associations of Canada-T1AC, the Alliance of Canadian Travel Associations-ACTA, Via Rail, and the Canadian Automobile Association. It is interesting to note that the minister responsible for tourism was in Newfoundland yesterday to meet with his provincial counterparts. There was meaningful discussion and productive dialogue.
It is interesting to note some of the recommendations that are being made to the government with regard to tourism. These are as follows: that the Canadian Government Office of Tourism-CGOT-be maintained, but that its role be examined and more clearly defined; that CGOT act as a co-ordinating body between the industry and the federal government departments, and between the federal and provincial departments of tourism; that CGOT spearhead the development of a national tourism development plan which does not operate in isolation from but, indeed, as a basic element of national policy on transportation, energy and general economic development; that there be a change of focus to include encouragement of tourism facilities development; that CGOT, in consultation with the industry and the provinces, develop a method for gathering and rapid dissemination of statistical information that will be of assistance to the tourism industry; that the title "Minister of State for International Trade" be changed to "minister of state for international trade and tourism"; that CGOT, in consultation with the provinces and the industry, co-ordinate the development of a national inventory of accommodation to determine the feasibility of a national rating system.
It has also been recommended that the minister express to the Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser) this committee's concern about the positive contribution that Parks Canada could make to the tourist industry. At the present time a great many of us feel it is too restricted. We also hope that the minister will request the Minister of Trans-
The Address-Mr. Darling
port (Mr. Mazankowski) to look into the effect of eliminating Canadian regulations hindering the entry of U.S. public charters on the Canadian air industry and tourism. It is also recommended that the minister strongly recommend to the Minister of Transport that any consideration of transportation policy should include passenger rail service and its impact on tourism.
I have been impressed with the down to earth approach of the present government. In this regard I am able to substantiate that it is the first time in the history of the Parry Sound coastguard base that a Minister of Transport from Ottawa has paid an official visit. This base, which serves the vital Great Lakes area, was visited by the Minister of Transport not too long ago, in fact on September 26. This is concrete evidence that this government wants to come to grips with the reality of problems facing Canadians by getting down to talking to the people. The previous government grew so arrogant and isolated in Ottawa it forgot that its mandate came from Canadians across the country. It is no wonder that such a harsh and deserved judgment was cast upon them in the last general election.
Another example of this new form of government is the recent visit by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Nielsen) to survey flood damage around the Lake Nipissing area.
What such visits symbolize is the desire on the part of the government to listen to the concerns of average Canadians, and to govern through consensus rather than dictation. The government in Ottawa cannot become isolated from the people like its predecessor, for it plans to stay in touch with the people.
Our national defence is being brought back on the rails by the very competent and able Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. McKinnon). I had the honour a week or so ago to announce on behalf of the Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs the expansion and upgrading of facilities, including the installation of new computer facilities in order to improve the surveillance of all Canadian air space. The move to establish the region operations control centre in North Bay to ensure the sovereignty of Canadian air space is a welcome move to all Canadians. The expenditure of $87 million on the upgrading of facilities and the employment of another 200 personnel in the area will certainly be a welcome boost to its economy.
While on the question of defence I must register my strong support for Canada to fulfil its commitment to participate in NATO with its other allies. Our participation in this vital body must be restored to the fullest. The recent ploys of President Brezhnev to reduce Soviet armed strength in Europe must not be taken at face value. The west must continue to be diligent and on guard even in times of detente.
The residents of Parry Sound-Muskoka have been concerned for quite some time now about the ill effects of acid rain and what it does to the many lakes in the area. I am delighted to see that the Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment has placed the question of acid rain high on his list for resolution, in consultation with our southerly neighbour. All of

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Darling
us wish him well in his deliberations and hope the efforts will bring good news.
As most have read in a recent issue of The Globe and Mail. a committee recently released a report which is certainly very disconcerting and shocking, especially in relation to my area which is one of the greatest tourist areas in the Dominion of Canada. The facts published in the paper were that about five million metric tons of sulphur dioxide is produced in Canada annually compared with about 25.7 million metric tons in the United States, and that of the U.S. emissions, about four million metric tons flow northward, compared with between
500,000	and 700,000 tonnes that blow south from Canada. It is very easy to see that even if we are able to reduce our emissions of sulphur dioxide we are not going to make much of an impact until the United States is willing to do the same.
There is certainly great concern among those of us in Ontario because about 140 lakes in Ontario, primarily in the Sudbury area and south, which includes my area, have been acidized to the point where they will not support certain types of fish. Let us hope something will be done about this. It is also noted that forest lands do not lend themselves to alternate uses. This fact was not given too much priority at the outset, but it is certainly something that gives us a great deal to think about.
The Progressive Conservative party, as we are aware, is the party of small business. It is this government which can best provide the ideal climate for growth of small businesses. After all, small businesses, whether in the tourist industry or any other, form the backbone of the economy of our country. Individual initiative is best reflected in the number of successful businesses that operate in this country. The task before us is to create a climate which will be attractive to new investment and will draw capital from all sources.
Another point on which I would like to touch briefly relates to the throne speech. The throne speech is not the be all and end all. It is merely an indication in the most general terms of what the government intends to do during its term in office. No one ought to expect dramatic announcements. The era of dramatic pronouncements faded away with the former government. The present government will obviously be making announcements, but on an ongoing basis. Not every item could have been detailed in the Speech from the Throne.
Apart from the economic crisis, the world today faces energy crises. Canada is well endowed with energy sources, ranging from the traditional coal to the tar sands. One must be pleased with the announcement in the Speech from the Throne of the intention to make Canada self-sufficient in energy by 1990. It is essential that we strive toward this goal in order to meet the energy challenge. In this regard I would like to mention the possible exploitation of peat or muskeg for energy use. Canada has a large reservoir of peat which is yet to be tapped. 1 have been in touch with various government departments to investigate this further.
I have for a long time been an advocate of some changes in spouse's allowances. I am, therefore, glad to note that Parliament will be asked to extend spouse's allowances in circum-

stances where they are now denied. 1 certainly welcome the introduction of the bill to amend the Old Age Security Act to bring in the necessary changes.
In the last few days there has been a lot of hysterical talk about the economic state of our country, talk that concentrated around the unfortunate increase in interest rates. Let me assure you that no one is happy with increases in interest rates. On the other hand, one cannot easily dismiss and overcome the mess in which the Liberals left the economy. A time period of a mere five months cannot remedy the Liberal's misguided economic policies of the last dozen years.

During my election campaign I pledged to fight against an increase in interest rates. I plan to continue this fight. As a former owner of a small business, I am well aware of the damage high interest rates can inflict upon small businesses. The cost of money, especially invested money, can be prohibitive, and often stifling to the growth or basic survival of small businesses.
Every Canadian is delighted to know that the Progressive Conservative government has kept its election promise to allow property and tax credits to come into operation at the earliest opportunity. This will make the dream of owning a home a reality for many Canadians in all income brackets. In addition, this program will provide stimulus to the construction and home furnishing industries. These industries are largely Canadian-owned and will be able to generate more jobs and income. The program will provide tax relief to existing home owners, as well as provide incentives that will make home ownership more attractive to prospective home buyers. This program will go a long way to making the basic necessity, shelter, available to a greater number of Canadians than ever before.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise and take part in this debate. First of all 1 want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald). Both members acquitted themselves well, and 1 am sure that they will continue to be an honour and a credit to their constituents in this chamber.
I want to congratulate, too, the Speaker of this House on his re-election and also congratulate as Acting Speaker, the representative for Carleton-Charlotte, who occupies the chair today.
This throne speech was not so much a throne speech as a university calendar. It offered us not so much a course of action as a course of study. It was not so much a series of proposals for moving our country forward as a series of seminars. We take our choice of a study on cultural policy, foreign ownership, the voluntary sector, and nuclear energy.
Of course there were some indications of good things to come. I was pleased, for example, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) pointed out, to see the
October 19, 1979

reference to improving the guidelines for the spouse's allowance. We will have to wait and see, of course, just what this means. Now that the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Graff-tey) has been removed from social programs, we might assume that a less hard line on selectivity will be taken on this and other social programs. Had he stayed where he was, no doubt we would have seen the application of Tory philosophy in the form of the means test, and we may still see it. But in my opinion this is not the route to go. The principles of universality in pensions and the spouse's allowance must never be tampered with.
Our senior citizens receive the pension not as a privilege but as a right. They deserve it because of their hard work throughout the years, and because of their contribution to society. They have paid into this scheme throughout their lives, and it is only fair and just that they all receive the pension in their later years. In any case, those in higher income brackets return the pension with their taxes. I hope the government will not be so foolish as to apply the means test to old age pensioners.
1 was also interested to hear that amendments would be made to veterans legislation. I sincerely hope that those measures will improve the lot of those who, in many cases, gave the best years of their lives for their country, and improve the lot also of their widows and dependants. However, I am fearful of this. This government has seen fit to insult our war veterans by abolishing the Ministry of Veterans Affairs as a full time portfolio. I can tell this government that veterans across this country will not take it lying down. They are not that kind of people, and neither are their sons or daughters. Certainly that is the word which I get from Newfoundland.
My colleague, the former member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe who now occupies a position in the other place, must have been shocked and angered to hear of the disregard for veterans' rights. For years in this House he fought incessantly to improve the lot of veterans like himself. I know that Senator Ches Carter, another champion of veterans, must have been shocked and angered as well. I can tell veterans that this party will not forget them and that we will speak on their behalf in this chamber to ensure that their interests are protected. War veterans have many vivid memories. They do not easily forget, and I can tell you they will not forget this government.
There are other measures that we look forward to with great interest. 1 welcome the extension of the power of Parliament and greater prominence given to private members' initiatives. I should congratulate, too, my own member of Parliament, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) on attaining the position he now occupies. 1 am sure that he will lend to that position the competence and dignity that he lent to his former position as House leader for the opposition. I welcome the reference in the throne speech to this measure.
I welcome too the suggestion of a youth employment secretariat and an employment strategy for women. 1 welcome the indication that the mandate of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be strengthened. This policy, a policy of our party, has been a tremendous asset to our people in improving services and expanding business in the Atlantic
The Address-Mr. Rompkey
provinces. These are positive and progressive measures and, provided they are well thought through, they should mean a great improvement.
Most of the campaign promises of this government were quickly forgotten, shelved, or "task-forced" once they got into office. One they did keep was the transfer of ownership of offshore resources of Newfoundland. There has been a strong positive reaction to this in our province. The House misunderstands the background of this. For decades my province has been a virtual ward of central Canada. Newfoundlanders have resented coming to Ottawa cap in hand for DREE agreements and other special concessions. They have never been satisfied that equalization payments have been such a large portion of the provincial budget. They have tried desperately to change an economy where unemployment insurance payments amount to $250 million a year, ranking after wages in transportation, and ahead of wages and salaries in fishing, mining, hospitals, and education. The amount from unemployment insurance is second only to the wages and salaries we get from biggest contributor of all to the provincial economy, and that is transportation.
We have always been an independent people in the best sense of the word, and we have never been afraid of hard work. Now, with clear indications of lucrative oil discoveries off our shores, Newfoundlanders and Labradorians see an opportunity to be self-reliant, self-supporting, and to contribute to, rather than draw from, the Canadian confederation. Of course we have contributed already our culture, our history, our songs and stories, and our traditions. When Canada is searching for an identity we have at least known who we are and where we come from. But now the emphasis must be on where we are going.
It is important for us to protect our way of life from the possible disruptions that the development of oil reserves can cause. Many of our people still live in small communities by the sea, sustained by a fishing economy and the strong bonds of community life. We must ensure that development is controlled, that it is not disruptive, and that it does not fracture or overwhelm the present way of life in Newfoundland. We must ensure that development is in the best interests of our people and that they will derive both immediate and lasting benefits from it. Therefore Newfoundland must have the power to look after its interest, but we will need to know a great deal more than what is contained in the correspondence between the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the premier. What has been agreed to is ownership. What is needed is control. These are interesting words-ownership, control, jurisdiction. How will they be interpreted in legislation and possible constitutional amendments? What will be the final deal? What will be the trade-offs? We will have to wait and see, and we will be watching closely.
Newfoundland and Labrador have legitimate needs, concerns, and rights flowing from their history, but Canada has needs and concerns too. If we want to be full Canadians in every sense of the word, surely we must act to strengthen Canada and not weaken it. Newfoundlanders and Labradori-

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Rompkey
arts may not be entirely satisfied with their present role in confederation, but they know full well the blessings of confederation, and they want very much to be a part of this country.
We are a people who have been known for our generosity and not our selfishness. I know that while Newfoundlanders want fiercely to defend their own interests, they will want to ensure that the country is strong too, in energy supply and in every other way. 1 believe that both of these aims can be achieved. But we will be watching closely as the negotiations go on between Ottawa and Newfoundland. I will be watching as a Newfoundlander and as a Canadian.
In the meantime we have serious problems that are of an immediate nature. Some of the oil discoveries are near our most historic and richest fishing grounds, the Grand Banks. There is imminent danger of the non-renewable resource destroying the renewable; and the fish, Mr. Speaker, will be there, we hope, long after the oil is gone. That is why, as I said earlier, controlled development is so important. Newfoundland and Labrador have depended on, and will continue to depend on fish as the mainstay of the economy. Therefore it is urgent that a proper contingency plan for dealing with oil spills be put in place. To my knowledge there is not one. I would suggest to my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) who, I know, shares my concern, that he see to it that such a plan, together with the necessary equipment placed in Newfoundland and Labrador, is put in operation immediately. He has the authority and the responsibility for this and he should act right away.
I want to congratulate my hon. colleague from St. John's East, Mr. Speaker, and to wish him well in his portfolio as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He is the first Newfoundlander to hold that portfolio. Much will be expected of him, in his home province as well as other areas of Canada. He has distinguished himself in this chamber as a member of Parliament. 1 hope his policies will be in line with his proposals. He will have some tough decisions to make. For our part, Mr. Speaker, we will be watching closely to see that those decisions are in the best interests of the fishermen and of the industry as a whole.
The Speech from the Throne tells us that a white paper will be produced on the fishery. After six months in office, when there are serious problems to be resolved the best this government can do is a white paper. No doubt this is all part of the plan for greater consultation. That is fine, Mr. Speaker, but 1 would ask the minister what consultation there was with inshore fishermen before large vessels were allowed back in the Gulf recently to fish for cod. This is an action which was undertaken without consultation. Yet the minister has said in his Corner Brook speech and elsewhere that emphasis must be given to the inshore fishery, and that the communities along the northeast coast of Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador must be protected.
We could not agree more, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, the minister in saying this, is continuing the policy of the former minister of
fisheries and of this party when we formed the administration. It is the right policy. The inshore fishery is important in the Atlantic provinces, not simply from the point of view of economics, but because of our very settlement and way of life. The inshore fishery and the Atlantic lifestyle are inseparably intertwined. To tamper with one is to undermine the other. That being the case, I ask how is it that there is no money in the small craft harbour budget to build and repair desperatly needed wharves and breakwaters? How is it that millions of dollars of Canada Works funds will go unspent because small craft harbours has no budget to complement the Canada Works funds as has been done over the past several years?
This party realized how important shore facilities were, and more than tripled the budget for them in recent years. I have brought this to the attention of the government before and nothing has been done. This is a serious matter, Mr. Speaker. I quote from a recent editorial in the St. John's Evening Telegram as follows:
Fishermen are in constant danger of losing not only their industrial property but also their lives, without adequate protection in many harbours.
It goes on to say:
But Newfoundland now does have two cabinet ministers in Ottawa, and they are in key positions in this respect, the Finance and Fisheries portfolios. They have already showed they can use their influence and knowledge to win support from their largely farm and city-oriented colleagues for other marine and related projects, and we hope they can be just as successful in getting action on the inadequacies of our small craft havens.
I echo those sentiments. But in all fairness it is the intransigence of the "Baron of Bay Street", the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), that is the real difficulty. He has not earned his reputation as "The Slasher" without hard work, Mr. Speaker. Not only has he slashed the public works budget for marine works, he has slashed millions of dollars in the vessel subsidies so that since June no inshore fishermen anywhere in the Atlantic region or Quebec have been able to replace vessels or to build new ones, and this at a time when the Atlantic fishery is more lucrative than ever.
Thanks to the establishment of the 200-mile limit by the previous Liberal government, the fish stocks are rebuilding, the price is good, and fishermen are optimistic. At least they were optimistic until the member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) got his hands on the tiller. Whatever he is doing, one thing is certain-he is not helping the fishermen. Even his leader has said that there are areas of the Canadian economy which need stimulation. The fishery is one of those, Mr. Speaker. 1 do not know how we can get that message to the President of the Treasury Board, but I can tell him that fishermen in Atlantic Canada and Quebec are frustrated and angry at the lack of support they are experiencing. I suspect it is true for fishermen and pleasure boat users who need small craft harbours in all areas of Canada. Consultation is fine, but it will not float; you cannot tie your boat to it, and you cannot eat it.
I would suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that he leave the towers of Bay Street and get into Atlantic Canada. If he does, he will find out for himself how disastrous his policies will be for the Fishermen in that area. If he goes to Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, he should take time for a trip on
[Mr. Rompkey. 1
October 19, 1979

the new Newfy Bullet. Yes, there is a Newfy Bullet, Mr. Speaker. It is not a big train, mind you. In fact, it is only one car. But it is beautifully outfitted. I listened to my colleagues in the House talk about more hopper cars for grain and the need for improvement in trains. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) mentioned that, and I certainly agree with him. We have a train now. It is confined to one car but it is a good car, a great car. It has sleeping and eating accommodations, a Cordon Bleu, even a telephone. And the President of the Treasury Board should not have any trouble getting on because the car is for VIP's only. It is for the movers and shakers in CN-at least the shakers-and the movers and shakers in the government. It is not the sort of thing you go fishing in on the 24th of May.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, they have made changes. It is no longer CN in Newfoundland but Terra Transport. Evidently, the President of the Treasury Board gave them enough money to buy a new name. No new track; no new cars; no new passengers; no new freight; a new name! I thought the Newfy joke was dead, Mr. Speaker, but it is not. It is alive and well, and running on a narrow gauge track!
The premier of the province was impressed. He said the announcement was merely cosmetic. He said, and I quote;
This latest announcement is a very silly attempt by CN to try and indicate to the people of Newfoundland that they are really doing something. The main problem we have right now is to get CN, who are totally responsible for the railway, to spend some money on it and try to make it a viable force in transportation in this province.
Right on, Mr. Speaker! We have heard from the Tory premier of Newfoundland and we could not agree more. That is a provincial premier speaking. So we have to sit up and take notice. The words of a provincial premier are not to be taken lightly or wantonly, but soberly and in the fear of God. And by the way, why was he not consulted about this? It was not "consult", Mr. Speaker; it was "insult". Is it any wonder that Newfoundland wants more control over its own affairs?
The new government has brought back the Newfy Bullet, Mr. Speaker. But how it is going to get half a million people into that one little car escapes me. Of course the people of Labrador will not be able to travel on it anyway because there are no tracks in Labrador, not even narrow gauge. My colleague, the hon. member from St. John's East, will be amused by the reversal of roles that goes on in this House. If he looks back through Hansard or, if I do, we will find a transposition of speeches of some years ago.
I want to talk about oil prices because the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka mentioned that. He talked about small businesses and the necessity to support them. I agree with that, but I wonder how we can support them with fuel oil prices rising 14 cents per gallon and gasoline rising 24 cents per gallon. That policy will have a disastrous effect in Atlantic Canada. I noticed that one cabinet minister is reported as saying that gasoline might even rise to $1.30 per gallon. Yesterday in Ottawa The Citizen reported someone as saying that within the next couple of years it might even rise to $1.45 per gallon.
The Address-Mr. Nickerson
It might interest the House of Commons to know, Mr. Speaker, that in Labrador city gasoline is already $1.39 a gallon, and fuel oil, 79 cents a gallon. In Goose Bay gasoline is over $1.40 a gallon. In Rigolet and St. Anthony it is in the same range. These are people who live in northern areas of the country where the winters are long and cold. To ask those people, most of whom do not have the capacity to pay, to shoulder the burden of higher fuel prices in the interests of conservation, is ludicrous. We are not talking about people who are wasting money on luxuries. We are talking about people who are working hard to make ends meet. This government says they should pay higher prices in the interests of conservation, in accordance with the demands of the Arab countries. There are other ways to achieve conservation, Mr. Speaker, more effective, less costly, and less harmful to primary producers and those at the lower end of the income scale.
What of small businesses? My friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka who preceded me mentioned those. They are struggling to survive, in danger of being swallowed up by large corporations. What will higher energy costs do to them? Besides adding to inflation, of which we have an overdose in the Atlantic, it will be an additional hurdle they have to overcome on the road to survival.
The real burden will be on the old, the widows, the disabled, the young, those who are on fixed incomes and low incomes, those who through no fault of their own cannot help themselves. Are we to tell old age pensioners that they must burn less gas in their power boats and skidoos? In fact, are we going to tell that to fishermen, loggers or miners? This government is. It says it will increase oil $4 a barrel by the end of 1980, adding about $100 to the average annual heating bill. The government may consult with the provinces on this one, but apart from Alberta it is unlikely it will get consent. Ministers are finally going to have to bite the bullet themselves.
My friend mentioned that the ministers of tourism are meeting in Newfoundland for the first time. That is good. However, what is their position on the increase in the cost of energy and what will it do to the tourism industry? The ministers of finance will also be meeting. It will be nice to see what comes out of St. John's.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for these few short minutes. I guess I will have to do a very major editing job on my speech. Unfortunately the first thing to go will have to be the congratulations to yourself. The second thing to go will be the geography lesson. We now get down to the main body of the speech.
A hundred years ago it was important that if Canada was to survive as a distinct nation the southern border be secured. Through the actions of great statesmen such as John A. Macdonald, this was achieved and it was Canada, not our

October 19, 1979
The Address-Mr. Nickerson
friends from the south, that took possession and developed the vacant prairies.
This having been done, it was then necessary to turn our eyes northward. However, it was not until that equally great Canadian statesman, the Right Hon. John George Diefen-baker, gave us his vision of the north, that Canadians as a whole began to realize that the destiny of this country lies in the effective use and occupation of Canada north of that narrow belt along the United States border.
Unfortunately the vision was transitory and became blurred when new governments took office, governments with a concept of Canada restricted to the limited geographical areas of central Quebec and Ontario from which they drew their political support. With a new and progressive government in office, we can look forward to a resurrection of the Diefen-baker vision, and we in the north, who have so much to offer, can look forward to playing our full role within the Canadian confederation.
His Excellency the Governor General in his throne speech outlined the two main fields in which progress has to be made in the northern territories. They are, of course, industrial and resource development on one hand, and constitutional development on the other.
There is no sound reason why prosperity should stop at the 60th parallel. The distribution of resources does not respect political boundaries. Resources extend on both sides of the border. There is no sound underlying economic reason why Alberta enjoys the highest standard of prosperity in this country whereas a few yards over the border the state of the economy is one of neglect and stagnation.
It is necessary that the Government of Canada help in the development of resources in the Northwest Territories, resources which it holds in trust for eventual Canadian provinces to be established in the north.
The throne speech refers specifically to the minerals industry. If you let us develop our oil fields and our gas fields, if you let us develop our uranium mines, if you let us harness our extensive hydro-electric resources, we can help Canada achieve its goal of energy self-sufficiency. If you allow us to develop our deposits of base and precious metals, our fishing industry and our fur industry, by exporting these products we can help Canada balance its books and reduce its international balance of payment deficit, and help restore international confidence in the Canadian currency.
If you allow us to develop our agriculture, our forests and our tourist industry, we will generate our own sources of revenue and become less dependent on the largesse of the southern Canadian taxpayer. All we want is the opportunity to do these things, and to be treated fairly and honestly in the same way as Canadians living in the southern provinces.
For these great things to happen, Canada must be prepared to invest in the provision of the necessary infrastructure. Roads have to be built, harbours and airports constructed, electric power made available at reasonable costs. What is probably more important is that present disincentives to investment in the north have to be removed. Our taxation policies and regulatory environment should be both certain, free from

arbitrary measures, and designed to encourage northern investment by Canadians. Our system of land tenure must ensure security of title, and our transportation policies must be designed so that products shipped both from and into the north can reach their destinations without being priced out of the marketplace.
In the very few minutes left 1 will turn to the subject of responsible government and the fact that northern Canadians to this very day are denied the full rights and privileges of Canadian citizenship. Is it conceivable that in the last quarter of the twentieth century Canada still governs part of its own country in this semi-colonial fashion?
Because we have to finish in about 60 seconds, I will dispense with the other things I had to say on the very important subject of constitutional development in the north. I would like to end by saying this. In the Northwest Territories the paternalistic socialism of the previous government has failed, and failed miserably. I am pround to stand here today as part of a new government, one unencumbered by the mistakes of the past, a government devoted to the active development of the Canadian north, a government that holds dear the principles of individual liberty and of private ownership, and most of all a government that recognizes the right of all Canadians, whether they live in the south or the north, to be masters of their own fate and controllers of their own political destiny.
